policies.title: Liability Insurance and Employer Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Agency Manager, Licensing Compliance Designee and payroll staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] holds the liability insurance Illinois requires, carries added coverage for agency-specific risks, and states clearly in every client agreement that the agency is the employer of its caregivers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a direct-service (employer) home services agency. It is not a Home Services Placement Agency, so the placement-agency limits in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.214 do not apply to it. The agency employs, supervises, schedules, disciplines and pays its caregivers, and it pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation coverage for them. The agency keeps evidence of liability insurance as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.90(a) and 245.30(b)(2), and it submitted that evidence with its initial application. The minimum policy limits are not stated in the codified text the agency has reviewed. A secondary source indicates $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 aggregate, but that figure has not been confirmed. Until IDPH confirms the required minimums in writing, the agency will carry limits that are not less than $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 aggregate and will confirm the requirement with IDPH. In addition, the agency carries hired and non-owned auto liability and employee-dishonesty (crime) coverage. Every client agreement states the employer responsibilities as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c).

definitions.definition: An agency that employs its caregivers and directs and supervises their work, as opposed to a placement agency that only refers workers.
Coverage for claims arising from vehicles the agency rents or that employees use for agency business but the agency does not own.
Coverage for loss of client or agency money or property caused by dishonest acts of employees.
Written evidence from the insurer or broker showing the coverage types, limits and effective dates.

procedures: 1. The governing body approves the insurance program and designates the Agency Manager to maintain it.

2. Before the initial application is submitted, the Agency Manager obtains a certificate of insurance for general and professional liability and the Licensing Compliance Designee includes it in the IDPH application packet (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.90(a)).

3. The Licensing Compliance Designee contacts IDPH (217-782-7412) to confirm the required minimum limits in writing and files the response. If IDPH's minimum is higher than the amounts in this policy, the Agency Manager raises coverage to the IDPH minimum before the next policy period or sooner if IDPH requires.

4. The Agency Manager asks the insurance broker to bind hired and non-owned auto liability and employee-dishonesty (crime) coverage, and confirms that the crime coverage covers theft from clients' homes by employees.
5. The Agency Manager obtains workers' compensation coverage for all employees as required by Illinois law and files the certificate.
6. The Agency Manager calendars every policy expiration date at 90 days and 30 days before expiration. The Licensing Compliance Designee uses the 90-day date for renewal planning under GOV-07.

7. At each renewal, the Agency Manager obtains an updated certificate and checks limits, effective dates and covered operations. Gaps are fixed before the old policy ends. The certificate is filed in the licensing file.
8. The Agency Manager gives the governing body an insurance summary (coverages, limits, carriers, expiration dates) at least annually.

9. Payroll staff withhold and pay employment taxes and Social Security taxes for every caregiver under agency payroll procedures (see PER-15). The agency does not treat caregivers as independent contractors for ordinary client care.

10. Intake staff use the agency's standard client agreement. Before anyone signs, the staff member checks that it states: assurance of compliance with the Act and the Health Care Worker Background Check Act; that the agency pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation; that the agency supervises workers and hires, fires and disciplines them; the charges, payment schedule and payee; the contract term and termination conditions; and contact information for concerns, complaints and questions.

11. The staff member explains the employer statement to the client or representative and tells them they do not need to pay caregiver taxes or workers' compensation for agency employees. The client or representative signs the agreement and receives a copy.
12. The agency uses no marketing wording that suggests it is a placement agency, and it does not charge a one-time placement fee in place of ongoing employment of its caregivers.

13. Employees report any accident, injury, property damage or claim to the Agency Manager the same day (see SAF-03). The Agency Manager notifies the insurer as the policy requires and logs the notice.

14. If any coverage is cancelled, not renewed or lapses, the Agency Manager informs the governing body the same day and takes immediate steps to restore coverage. The governing body decides whether services must be suspended while coverage is restored, and the Designee consults IDPH on any required notice.

Buys and maintains all coverage, tracks expirations and reports claims and incidents to the insurer.
Includes insurance evidence in IDPH submissions and confirms IDPH's minimum limits.
Withhold and remit employment and Social Security taxes and keep workers' compensation current.
Use the standard client agreement and explain the employer statement to clients.

IDPH written confirmation of minimum limits

Claim and incident notices to insurers

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All employees, with intake staff, the Agency Manager and caregivers having specific duties
policies.purpose: To make sure every [AGENCY NAME] client knows their rights and responsibilities in writing before services begin, to train caregivers in those rights every year, and to ensure no one is refused service because of a protected characteristic.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects the dignity, independence, self-determination, privacy, choice and rights of every client. The agency gives each client or representative a written Client Rights and Responsibilities statement together with the client agreement (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c)). Every worker receives training on these topics each year (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(f)). The agency will not refuse service to anyone on the basis of the protected classes listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d)). The agency accepts clients based on need for non-medical help and does not provide medical services.

definitions.definition: A person who receives non-medical in-home services from [AGENCY NAME].
A person legally authorized or chosen by the client to act or receive information for the client.
The client's right to make their own choices about how services are provided, including the right to decline a service.
The characteristics listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q), on which the agency may not base a refusal of service.

procedures: 1. The Agency Manager maintains the Client Rights and Responsibilities statement in plain language and in the languages the agency serves (see CR-05). It is reviewed at the annual policy review under GOV-03.

2. The statement lists the client's rights: to be treated with dignity and respect; to independence, self-determination and choice, including taking part in the service plan and refusing services; to privacy and confidentiality of person, home and records; to be free from abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination; to be told in advance about charges and any change in charges; to receive at least 7 working days' written notice, with reasons, before the agency ends services, except where worker safety is at risk; to make a complaint without retaliation; and to contact IDPH.

3. The statement lists the client's responsibilities: to give accurate information about needs and contacts; to provide a safe home for caregivers; to tell the agency about changes in condition or schedule; to pay as agreed; and to treat caregivers with respect.

4. Intake staff hand every client or representative the statement along with the signed client agreement at or before the first visit, and go through it verbally in the client's preferred language or by interpreter.

5. The client or representative signs an acknowledgment of receipt. Intake staff file it in the client record and give a copy to the client. If the client declines to sign, staff document the date and reason.
6. The statement and agreement include how to make a complaint (see CR-02), the agency's contact numbers (see GOV-08) and IDPH's Home Services Program number, 217-782-7412 (TTY 800-547-0466).

7. Intake staff screen referrals only for the need for non-medical help, safety of the home setting and the agency's ability to meet the documented needs (see SVC-02). They do not consider protected classes. If the agency cannot serve a person, staff state the non-discriminatory reason in the intake record and refer the person to another provider.
8. The Agency Manager reviews every declined or deferred referral weekly to check that the reason is documented and does not involve a protected class. Concerns are escalated to the governing body.

9. The Training Coordinator includes client dignity, independence, self-determination, privacy, choice and rights in each caregiver's annual training and records the date and hours (see PER-05 and PER-06). The topic is also covered at orientation (see PER-03).
10. Supervisors check how caregivers respect rights during supervisory visits (see SVC-04 and SVC-05), looking for dignity, privacy during personal care, and client choice. Findings are documented.

11. Staff who see or hear about a rights violation report it to the Agency Manager the same day. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01. A rights violation by an employee is handled under PER-13.
12. The Agency Manager records rights-related complaints and findings and provides them to the quality improvement program every quarter (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the rights statement, reviews declined referrals and investigates rights concerns.
Provide and explain the statement, obtain the signed acknowledgment and apply non-discriminatory acceptance practices.
Delivers and records annual training on rights.
Observe respect for client rights in the home and document findings.
Honor client rights in every visit and report violations.

documentation: Current Client Rights and Responsibilities statement
Signed acknowledgment of receipt in each client record
Declined and deferred referral log with stated reasons
Annual training records showing the rights topic
Supervisory visit notes on rights
Complaint and rights-concern records

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints (Complaint Resolution Policy)
policies.applies_to: All employees, clients, client representatives and client advocates
policies.purpose: To give clients and their advocates a clear, written way to raise concerns with [AGENCY NAME] and have them looked into and answered promptly, and to meet the requirement for a written complaint-resolution policy.
policies.policy: This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(b)(3) and IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item 245.30 b) 3) — Initial applicants only: complaint resolution policy. [AGENCY NAME] maintains this written complaint-resolution policy between the agency and its clients and client advocates. The client agreement lists contact information for concerns, complaints and questions (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c)(6)). The agency accepts complaints in any form (spoken, written or through a representative or advocate), investigates every complaint, records each one in a complaint log (date received, investigation, resolution and response to the client), and does not retaliate against anyone who complains. Clients are told that they may also contact IDPH at any time, whether or not they have used the agency's process. A complaint that involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is handled under SAF-01 and SAF-02.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency, its services, its caregivers or its billing, made by a client, representative or advocate.
A person or organization who speaks for a client, such as a family member, guardian, friend, care coordinator or ombudsman.
The agency's running record of complaints showing date received, investigation, resolution and response to the client.
Any adverse action, such as reduced service, schedule changes or threats, taken because a person made a complaint.

procedures: 1. The Agency Manager designates a Complaint Coordinator ([COMPLAINT COORDINATOR NAME]) and a back-up, and posts their names and [PHONE] in the client agreement and handbook.

2. Intake staff give each client or representative the written complaint-resolution policy with the client agreement. It lists the agency telephone number, the after-hours number (see GOV-08), the mailing address [ADDRESS], and IDPH's Home Services Program number 217-782-7412 (TTY 800-547-0466), as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c)(6).

3. For clients served through the IDoA Community Care Program, the handbook also gives the Senior HelpLine, 1-800-252-8966, and tells clients they may raise concerns with their Care Coordination Unit.

4. Any employee who receives a complaint, whether by phone, in person, in writing or through a caregiver, writes down the complainant's name, client name, date, and what was said, and gives it to the Complaint Coordinator the same business day.
5. The Complaint Coordinator enters the complaint in the complaint log the day it is received, with a complaint number.
6. The Complaint Coordinator acknowledges the complaint to the client or advocate within 2 business days, by the person's preferred method, and explains the next steps.

7. The Complaint Coordinator screens each complaint on the day received for possible abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury or immediate danger. If any is possible, the Coordinator acts under SAF-01, SAF-02 and SAF-03 first. A client in immediate danger is told to call 911.

8. The Complaint Coordinator investigates, which may include interviewing the client, caregiver and supervisor, reviewing visit notes and schedules, and visiting the home. The Coordinator records the investigation steps and findings in the log. People who are the subject of the complaint do not take part in the investigation.
9. The Complaint Coordinator aims to resolve the complaint within 14 calendar days. If more time is needed, the Coordinator tells the client in writing why and gives a new target date.

10. The Coordinator gives the client or advocate a response, spoken and then in writing, that states what was found, what action was taken or why none was taken, and how to take the matter further. The response date is recorded in the log.

11. If the client is not satisfied, the Coordinator refers the matter to the Agency Manager for review within 5 business days. The Manager decides after review and tells the client. The client is again told they may contact IDPH, and, for CCP clients, the Care Coordination Unit.

12. Corrective action involving staff, such as retraining or discipline, is taken under PER-13 and recorded in the personnel file but not in the client's complaint response beyond a general statement that action was taken.
13. No employee may retaliate against a complainant. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the Agency Manager and investigated as a new complaint.

14. The Agency Manager reviews the complaint log at least quarterly for patterns (same caregiver, same issue, slow response) and reports to the governing body and the quality improvement program (see GOV-04).
15. If IDPH asks about a complaint, the Agency Manager gives IDPH the complaint file as set out in GOV-06.
16. The agency keeps complaint records for at least 2 years after the last date of service for the client concerned (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Logs, screens, investigates and answers every complaint on time and tracks open items.
Reviews unresolved complaints, prevents retaliation and reports patterns to the governing body.
Pass every complaint to the Complaint Coordinator the same business day and never discourage or retaliate against a complainant.
Give the policy to each client and explain how to complain, including the right to contact IDPH.
Reviews complaint trends and ensures corrective action.

documentation: Written complaint-resolution policy given to clients
Complaint log (date received, investigation, resolution, response to client)
Acknowledgment and resolution letters
Investigation notes and supporting records
Client agreement showing complaint contact information
Quarterly complaint trend report

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and volunteers with access to client or personnel information
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client and personnel information and to set rules for the use, removal and release of client records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written confidentiality policy covering the use, removal and release of client records, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(j). The office protects the confidentiality of records (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(a)). Personnel records are kept confidential (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(c)(1)(G)). Employees use client information only as needed to do their jobs. Client records are not removed from the office, and information is not released, except as this policy allows. HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) applies if the agency is a covered entity, for example because it bills Medicaid electronically. The governing body has the Agency Manager make and document that determination, and if the agency is a covered entity, it follows the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530. This includes a designated privacy official, workforce training, safeguards, a complaint process and sanctions for violations. Even if the agency is not a covered entity, it applies the standards in this policy to all client information.

definitions.definition: Information kept for each client, including identifying data, representative and emergency contacts, service plan, signed agreement and visit documentation.
A health plan, clearinghouse, or health care provider that sends certain transactions electronically (such as Medicaid billing) and is subject to HIPAA.
Giving a client's information to anyone outside the agency.
Taking client records, in paper or electronic form, out of the office.
Employee file information including application, background check, training, health, evaluation and wage records.

procedures: 1. The Agency Manager documents in writing, with date, whether [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, because it bills Medicaid or other payers electronically), and reviews that decision each year and whenever billing methods change.
2. The Agency Manager names a Privacy Official ([PRIVACY OFFICIAL NAME]) who is responsible for this policy and receives privacy complaints and questions.

3. Intake staff give each client or representative a written statement of how the agency uses and shares information and, if the agency is a covered entity, the notice required by HIPAA. They record the date it was given in the client record.

4. Access to client records is limited by job. Caregivers see only the service plan and information about their own clients. Office staff see only what their duties need. Access to electronic records requires an individual password.

5. Paper client records are kept in locked cabinets in the office. Electronic records are kept in a password-protected system with automatic log-off. The Agency Manager reviews access to electronic records and removes former employees' access on or before their last day.

6. Client records may be removed from the office only with the Agency Manager's approval, only for a stated purpose (such as a supervisory visit, a scheduled audit or a legal demand) and only in a locked bag or secure device. Staff record the date removed and returned on the Record Removal Log.

7. Caregivers keep any client documents they carry or leave in the home in a way that others cannot see, return them to the office as directed, and never copy or photograph client information on a personal device.

8. Information is released outside the agency only with the client's or representative's written, signed and dated authorization, with these exceptions: reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation under SAF-01; requests from IDPH or other government agencies with legal authority, including surveyors; payer requests needed for authorized payment or monitoring (such as IDoA or DHS-DRS); medical emergencies; and legal process reviewed by the Agency Manager.

9. Staff who receive a records request send it to the Privacy Official without answering it. The Privacy Official verifies identity and authority, releases only the minimum information needed, and records each release (date, requester, information, reason) in the client record.

10. When records are faxed, staff use non-thermal paper for copies kept in the record, confirm the receiving number first and use a cover sheet with a confidentiality notice (see 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(h)-(j)). Staff send email containing client information only through the agency's secure system.

11. Employees do not discuss clients in public, with family not authorized by the client, or on social media or personal messaging. Staff must not post names, photographs or any details of clients or their homes.

12. Personnel records are kept in locked files separate from client records. Access is limited to the Agency Manager, authorized human resources staff and the employee for their own file. Release is only with the employee's written consent or as required by law, including IDPH review during surveys (see PER-11).
13. The Training Coordinator trains each employee on this policy at orientation and again each year, and keeps the signed confidentiality agreement in the personnel file (see PER-03 and PER-05).

14. Any employee who learns of a lost record, wrongly sent information, unauthorized access or other privacy incident reports it to the Privacy Official the same day. The Privacy Official investigates, limits further harm, tells the affected client or representative, and records the incident under SAF-03. The agency also meets any notice duty that applies to it under HIPAA or state law.
15. Employees who violate this policy are disciplined under PER-13, up to and including termination. Staff are not retaliated against for good-faith reports.

16. Client records are kept for at least 2 years after the last date of service, in hard copy or electronic form, and are destroyed securely after that period unless a legal hold applies (see REC-01).

17. The Privacy Official reviews this policy annually, tests record security (locks, passwords, access lists) and reports results to the governing body and the quality improvement program (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Oversees this policy, handles records requests and privacy incidents and reviews access.
Makes the covered-entity determination, approves record removal and protects the office and personnel files.
Secure records, verify requests and log releases and removals.
Protect client information in the home and on the job and report incidents the same day.
Trains staff and collects signed confidentiality agreements.

documentation: Written covered-entity determination and annual review
Signed employee confidentiality agreements
Authorization forms and release log
Record Removal Log

Training records on privacy and confidentiality
Client acknowledgment of privacy information

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, contracted workers, volunteers, supervisors and managers who have contact with clients, client property or client financial information.
policies.purpose: To protect clients' money, property and financial identity from loss, misuse and exploitation, and to make sure any suspected financial exploitation is reported to the correct authorities and investigated as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats a client's money, property, credit cards, checks and financial information as the client's alone. Employees may not borrow from clients, accept gifts from clients, or hold, keep or use a client's credit cards, debit cards, checks or PIN numbers. Financial exploitation of a client is a reportable event under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250 and the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20). On reasonable suspicion of financial exploitation of a client aged 60 or older, a client with a disability, or any 'eligible adult' under 320 ILCS 20, [AGENCY NAME] notifies the elder abuse provider agency designated by the Illinois Department on Aging (IDoA) or the Area Agency on Aging. If the victim is under 18, the agency calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. An employee accused of exploiting a client is removed from direct client contact immediately while the matter is investigated. Mandated-reporter duties under 320 ILCS 20 remain in force and are not replaced by any internal step in this policy. This policy works with SAF-01 (Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting) and SAF-02 (Abuse Investigations and Law Enforcement Notification).

definitions.definition: The misuse, taking or control of a client's money, property, benefits or financial identity, whether by force, deception, undue influence or by taking advantage of the client's condition.

A person who qualifies for protection under the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20), including adults with disabilities and persons aged 60 or older who may be subject to abuse, neglect or exploitation.
The agency designated by IDoA, or the Area Agency on Aging, to receive and respond to reports of abuse, neglect and financial exploitation of eligible adults.
Money, goods, services, loans, bequests or any other thing of value offered by a client or the client's family to an employee, other than the agency's authorized fee.

procedures: At hire and at orientation (PER-03), the Agency Manager reviews this policy with every employee and obtains a signed acknowledgment that the employee will not borrow from clients, accept gifts, or hold clients' credit cards, checks or PIN numbers. The signed acknowledgment is filed in the personnel record.
Employees do not ask clients for loans, advances, purchases on credit or any other financial favor, and do not lend their own money to clients.

Employees decline all gifts, including cash, gift cards, jewelry, household items, vehicles and promises of wills or bequests. The employee politely tells the client that agency policy does not allow gifts. If declining would seriously distress the client, the employee accepts nothing, leaves the item in the home, and tells the supervisor the same day.

Employees never hold, keep, carry or use a client's credit card, debit card, checks, bank passwords or PIN numbers, and never add themselves to a client's accounts, titles, powers of attorney or beneficiary designations.

When a service plan calls for shopping, the client or representative decides what is bought. The employee uses only cash the client gives for that trip, keeps every receipt, and returns the change and receipts to the client at the end of the trip. The employee records the amount received, the amount spent and the change returned on the visit record (REC-04), and the client or representative initials it when able.

Employees do not sign a client's name, cash a client's checks, make deposits or withdrawals, pay the client's bills, or access a client's online accounts. Employees do not use a client's phone, car, supplies or property for personal use.
Employees do not take client property out of the home except as written in the service plan (for example, a shopping list or laundry), and they return it the same day.

During assessments and supervisory visits (SVC-02, SVC-04), the supervisor looks for warning signs of exploitation: missing money or belongings, unexplained withdrawals, new names on accounts, unpaid bills despite adequate income, sudden changes in a will or power of attorney, or pressure from any person on the client's finances. The supervisor documents what was seen.

Any employee who suspects financial exploitation by anyone, including a co-worker, family member or other person, reports it immediately to the Agency Manager and also to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging [PHONE]. The employee does not wait for the agency to investigate or confirm the suspicion first, and does not confront the suspected person.

The Agency Manager makes or confirms the report to the elder abuse provider agency on the day the suspicion is raised. If the client is under 18, the Agency Manager calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. If a crime is in progress or the client is in immediate danger, anyone present calls 911.

If an employee is the alleged perpetrator, the Agency Manager removes the employee from all direct client contact immediately, before any investigation interview takes place, and assigns a replacement caregiver for the client.

The Agency Manager documents each report: the date and time, who reported, who received the report, the facts observed, and the agency's response. Report documentation is kept on the agency's premises for 12 months.

The Agency Manager completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report, following SAF-02. The report is sent to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, and a copy is kept for 12 months.
The Agency Manager follows up on any protective actions with the client or representative and the elder abuse provider agency, and notifies the client's payer program if required (SVC-13).
The agency takes no retaliation against any employee or client who reports in good faith. Any retaliation is itself a violation of agency policy and is subject to discipline up to termination.

Employees who violate this policy are disciplined up to and including termination, and the Administrator refers matters involving suspected crimes to law enforcement and notifies IDPH as required by GOV-06 and GOV-07.
The Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04) reviews the number and outcome of financial exploitation reports and any policy exceptions at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, ensures reports are made and investigated, refers suspected crimes to law enforcement, and ensures no retaliation.

Trains staff, collects acknowledgments, receives and makes reports, removes accused employees from client contact, completes the written investigation within 14 days and sends it to IDPH within 24 hours of completion.
Watch for warning signs during supervisory visits, check shopping and receipt records, and report concerns the same day.
Do not borrow, accept gifts or hold cards or checks; keep receipts; and report any reasonable suspicion immediately to management and to the elder abuse provider agency.

documentation: Signed employee acknowledgment of this policy (personnel record)
Shopping and cash-handling entries and receipts on visit records
Report log and each report to the elder abuse provider agency or DCFS (kept on premises 12 months)
Written investigation report and IDPH transmittal (copy kept 12 months)
Documentation of removal of an accused employee from client contact
Annual QI summary of reports

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, contracted workers and managers involved in client intake, service delivery, hiring, supervision and communication with clients and families.
policies.purpose: To ensure that no person is refused service, treated differently or denied communication access because of a protected characteristic, language or disability, and that the agency's personnel practices comply with the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not refuse service to anyone on the basis of any protected class listed in the Illinois Human Rights Act, 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q), as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d). Acceptance is decided only on the client's need for non-medical help and the agency's ability to meet that need safely within the scope of services. The agency's personnel policies provide for compliance with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(c)(1)(F)) in recruiting, hiring, assignment, pay, training, discipline and termination. Consistent with Title VI (42 USC 2000d) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12182), the agency provides interpreters or translated documents to clients with limited English proficiency, and communication aids to clients with disabilities, at no charge to the client.

definitions.definition: A characteristic protected from discrimination under 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) and the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as applied to service refusal and employment under this policy.
A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to communicate effectively about care, rights and services.

A device or service that makes communication effective for a person with a hearing, vision, speech or cognitive disability, such as a sign language interpreter, large-print or Braille documents, written notes, relay services or a reading of documents aloud.
A person competent in both languages and in the terms used in care, who has no conflict of interest with the client; not a minor child.

procedures: The Administrator posts and distributes a nondiscrimination statement, in the languages most common in the service area, in the office, on the agency's website and in the client packet. The statement says that service is not refused on any protected-class basis and says how to file a complaint with the agency (CR-02).

At intake (SVC-02), the intake staff member asks every client the language in which the client prefers to speak and read, and whether the client needs any communication aid. The answers are recorded in the client record and on the service plan.

When a client has LEP, the Agency Manager arranges a qualified interpreter or a translated copy of the client agreement, rights and responsibilities, service plan and complaint information at no charge. The agency may use a bilingual employee who has been shown to be fluent. The agency does not require the client to supply an interpreter.

Family members or friends interpret only if the client asks for that in private, after being told a free interpreter is available. The request is documented. Minor children are not used to interpret except in an emergency when no one else is available.

When a client has a hearing, vision, speech, cognitive or other disability affecting communication, the Agency Manager provides an effective communication aid at no charge, such as a sign language interpreter, large-print documents or reading documents aloud. The agency does not add a surcharge for these aids.
The Agency Manager keeps a list of interpreter and translation resources, including a telephone interpreter service, and makes the list available to all supervisors and the on-call contact.

Service refusal: the Agency Manager may decline a referral only for a documented, nondiscriminatory reason, such as a need for medical services outside the agency's scope (SVC-01, SVC-02), a client's non-payment, or a documented risk to worker safety. Every refusal is recorded on the intake log with the specific reason. No referral is declined because of a protected characteristic.
The Administrator reviews the intake log at least quarterly to confirm that no refusal pattern suggests discrimination, and reports the review to the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04).

Caregiver assignments are based on skills, availability and the client's reasonable preferences about gender for personal care or language needs. The agency does not allow assignment requests to be used to discriminate against employees. When a client asks that a caregiver not be assigned for a reason that would be unlawful discrimination, the Agency Manager explains agency policy to the client and documents the conversation.
Employees are trained in orientation (PER-03) on treating all clients with dignity, on the nondiscrimination statement, on how to reach an interpreter, and on reporting discrimination.

Hiring, promotion, pay, scheduling, training, discipline and termination decisions follow the personnel policies (PER-09, PER-13) and are made without regard to protected characteristics, in compliance with the Civil Rights Act of 1964 as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(c)(1)(F).

Reasonable accommodations are provided to employees and applicants with disabilities, and to clients as needed for them to receive and understand services, unless doing so would fundamentally alter the service or create an undue burden as defined by law. The Administrator makes the final decision and documents the reasons if an accommodation is denied.

Any employee, client or family member may report discrimination to any supervisor, to the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE], or through the complaint process in CR-02. The agency does not retaliate against anyone who reports.
The Administrator reviews each discrimination complaint, documents the findings and corrective actions, and sends the complaint record to the Quality Improvement Program.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, reviews refusals and complaints, ensures hiring and employment practices comply with the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and decides on accommodations.
Record language and communication needs, arrange free interpreters and aids, document the reason for any declined referral.
Confirm during supervisory visits that communication needs are being met and that the client is treated with respect.
Treat all clients with respect, use interpreter services as arranged, and report discrimination or communication barriers.

documentation: Nondiscrimination statement and posting record
Language and communication-aid preference in client record
Interpreter or translation log, including the language, date and provider
Intake log with reasons for any referral declined
Quarterly intake-log review
Discrimination complaint file and corrective actions
Orientation training record on nondiscrimination

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] clients and representatives; the Administrator, Agency Manager, intake and billing staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure every client receives, before services begin, a written agreement that discloses what services are offered, who is responsible for what, what will be charged and how to raise concerns, and to meet the IDPH application requirement for a copy of the current client contract.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, 'Required documentation (all applicants) - 245.220': a copy of the current client contract per 245.220 for Home Services, plus any attachments noted in the contract (rights and responsibilities, service plan, rate sheet). [AGENCY NAME] signs a written client agreement with every client or representative before services start. The agreement includes, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c): (1) an assurance of compliance with the Home Health, Home Services, and Home Nursing Agency Licensing Act, including the Health Care Worker Background Check Act; (2) who pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation; (3) who supervises workers and who hires, fires and disciplines them; (4) charges, payment schedule and payee; (5) the contract term and conditions for termination; and (6) contact information for concerns, complaints and questions. Before contracting, with the signed contract, and whenever it changes, the agency gives the client the list of services offered and the scope of work for each service (245.210(b)). The agency attaches the rights and responsibilities statement, the service plan and the rate sheet to the agreement, and submits a copy of the current contract with its IDPH application.

definitions.definition: The written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or representative stating the terms of service. It is part of the client record.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as a guardian or agent under a power of attorney, or another person the client has designated in writing.
The written schedule of the agency's charges, including hourly rates, minimums, any holiday or other differentials, and billing terms.

The person or program responsible for payment: the client or family (private pay), private insurance, the IDoA Community Care Program (CCP) or the DHS Division of Rehabilitation Services Home Services Program (HSP).

procedures: The Administrator approves the standard client agreement template, and verifies against the full text of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.220 and 245.210(c) that it contains every required element. The Administrator re-checks the template at least annually and after any rule change (GOV-03).

Before the contract is signed, the Agency Manager gives the client or representative the current list of services offered, with the scope of work for each service (see SVC-01), the rights and responsibilities statement (CR-01), the complaint procedure (CR-02), the privacy notice (CR-03) and the rate sheet. The date given is recorded.

The Agency Manager reviews the agreement with the client or representative in plain language, in the client's preferred language or with the interpreter arranged under CR-05, and answers questions. The client is given time to read the agreement and is not pressured to sign.
The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Home Health, Home Services, and Home Nursing Agency Licensing Act and the Health Care Worker Background Check Act.

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME], as the employer of its workers, pays employment taxes, Social Security taxes and workers' compensation, unless the Administrator has approved a different arrangement and written it into the agreement (GOV-09, PER-15).
The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] supervises the workers and is responsible for hiring, firing and disciplining them, and that the client does not direct payroll or discipline.

The agreement states the charges, the payment schedule and the payee. The rate sheet lists the private-pay hourly rate and any minimum hours, differentials or other charges. For CCP and HSP clients, the agreement identifies the program as payer and states that the program's published rates apply. As published when this manual was adopted, the IDoA CCP in-home service rate is $30.80 per hour ($32.57 per hour with insurance), and HSP maximum unit prices include homemaker at $30.80 per hour and personal assistant at $20.00 per hour. The billing staff verify the current published rates before each rate sheet is issued.

The agreement states the term of the contract and the conditions for termination by either party. Termination by the agency follows SVC-12: at least 7 working days' written notice with a stated reason, except where worker safety is at risk, in which case the risk is documented.

The agreement gives complaint and question contacts: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE], [ADDRESS], and the IDPH complaint contact (GOV-06, CR-02), with a statement that the client may complain without fear of retaliation.
The client or representative and an agency representative sign and date the agreement. The client receives a complete signed copy, including all attachments, before the first visit.
The Agency Manager files the original agreement in the client record (REC-01) and enters the payer, start date and any attachments.

When the services list, scope of work, rates or any other term changes, the Agency Manager gives the client the revised list or rate sheet in writing at least 30 days before the change takes effect (or immediately for a change the client requests), and obtains a signed amendment. A revised services list is given to the client whenever it changes.

Billing staff issue invoices at the interval set in the agreement. Each invoice lists dates, hours, rate and total, and is based on the electronic visit or time records (SVC-10, REC-04). Billing staff review any disputed charge within [10] business days and correct errors promptly with a written credit or refund.

For CCP and HSP clients, billing follows program authorizations and rules (SVC-13). The agency does not bill the client for any amount the program pays, except for any client share set by the program.

The Administrator keeps a current copy of the standard contract with its attachments (rights and responsibilities, service plan form, rate sheet) in the licensing file, and submits it with the IDPH application and whenever the agency is surveyed (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement template and rate sheet, verifies compliance with 245.210(c) and 245.220, and submits the contract with the IDPH application.
Reviews the agreement with each client, gives the services list and attachments, obtains signatures and files the agreement.
Prepare accurate invoices from visit records, verify program rates, and resolve disputes.
Reads and signs the agreement, pays as agreed, and gives notice as required in the agreement.

documentation: Signed client agreement with all attachments (rights and responsibilities, service plan, rate sheet) in the client record
Record of the date the services list and scope of work were given and of any later changes
Signed amendments for rate or service changes
Rate sheet history and program rate verification
Invoices and dispute resolutions
Copy of the current contract in the IDPH licensing file

policies.title: Scope of Services — What Caregivers May and May Not Do
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] home services workers, supervisors, intake staff and managers.
policies.purpose: To define the non-medical services [AGENCY NAME] provides, to set the limits on what caregivers may and may not do, and to supply the scope of services required with the IDPH application.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, 'Required documentation (all applicants) - 245.40 c)': a copy of the agency's scope of services. [AGENCY NAME] provides home services only, as defined in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c): help with activities of daily living (ADLs), housekeeping, personal laundry and companionship in the client's residence. Home services exclude anything that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee. Workers may observe and report changes in client functioning, do chores and meal preparation, help with shopping and appointments, provide companionship, document services, and assist with ADLs and personal care. Workers perform services only as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245 allows. The agency keeps a list of the services it offers and the scope of work for each, and gives it to clients before contracting, with the signed contract, and whenever it changes (245.210(a)-(b)). Task limits in 245.40(c)(4) apply to skin care, ambulation, bathing, dressing and compression garments, exercise, feeding and thickener, hair care, mouth care, nail care, positioning, shaving and toileting. Most of these tasks require (1) client or representative feedback, (2) worker training in the method, and (3) an agency competency evaluation; several also require a health care professional's order. Workers may not perform passive range of motion, nail trimming or skilled skin care, and may not perform or provide medication setup.

definitions.definition: Help with ADLs, housekeeping, personal laundry and companionship in the client's residence. Home services exclude anything that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee.
Basic self-care activities such as bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, eating, ambulation and transfers, as limited by 245.40(c)(4).
The agency's documented check, before first assignment, that a worker can correctly perform a task in the approved method (PER-04).
A written or documented instruction from a licensed professional authorized to give it, needed for certain tasks under 245.40(c)(4).
The agency's written list of the services it offers and the scope of work for each.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the agency's written scope of services: a list of each service offered, with the scope of work for each. It covers ADL support, personal care, medication reminding, housekeeping, personal laundry, meal preparation, shopping, transportation to appointments, household records and companionship, limited to what the agency actually offers. The scope is dated and version-controlled (GOV-03).
The Administrator provides a copy of the scope of services with the IDPH application and for each survey (GOV-02, GOV-06).

Intake staff give the current list of services and scope of work to each prospective client before contracting and again with the signed contract (CR-06). Any change to the list is given to the clients concerned, in writing, when it changes.

The Agency Manager builds a task matrix from the full text of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4), covering every task item in the rule, listing for each: whether it is permitted, the conditions (client or representative feedback, worker training, agency competency evaluation, health care professional's order if required) and the required documentation. The Administrator reviews the matrix against the rule text at least annually and after any amendment. A task is not performed by workers unless the matrix shows it is permitted.
Workers perform only tasks listed in the client's service plan (SVC-03). The plan may not include a task outside the worker scope in 245.40(c)(4).

Before a worker performs any task that needs client or representative feedback, worker training and a competency evaluation, the supervisor confirms that all three are done and documented. Where a health care professional's order is also required, the supervisor confirms the order is on file in the client record before the task is assigned.

Workers do not provide medical services or anything that requires a Nurse Practice Act licensee. For example, workers do not give injections, administer medications, change sterile dressings, provide wound care, or perform catheter, ostomy, tube-feeding or suctioning care.

Workers do not perform passive range of motion, do not trim nails, and do not provide skilled skin care. Workers may perform only the approved skin, nail, hair and mouth care described in the task matrix.

Workers do not perform or provide medication setup. A worker may remind a client about medications only when they were pre-selected by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist and are in containers other than prescription bottles, such as medication minders. Medication reminding is handled under SVC-06.
Positioning, transfers and oxygen-related support are limited as stated in SVC-07.
Workers observe and report changes in the client's functioning. A worker who sees a change in condition reports it to the supervisor the same day, or immediately if urgent (SVC-11).

When a client or family member asks a worker to do something outside the scope, the worker says politely that it is outside what the agency may do, does not perform it, and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor documents the request and, as appropriate, refers the client to a licensed provider, to the client's physician or to a licensed home health agency.
A worker who is unsure whether a task is permitted does not perform it and calls the supervisor or on-call contact (GOV-08) for direction.
Supervisors check, during supervisory visits (SVC-04, SVC-05), that workers are performing only permitted tasks in the approved way, and retrain or take corrective action when they are not.
If a client's needs grow beyond the home services scope, the Agency Manager follows SVC-02, SVC-03 and SVC-12 to revise the plan, help arrange other services, or discharge with proper notice.

Violations of this policy, such as performing a prohibited task, are reported to the Administrator and may result in corrective action up to termination, and are reviewed by the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves and maintains the scope of services and task matrix, submits the scope to IDPH, and reviews them against the rules at least annually.
Verify feedback, training, competency and orders before assigning limited tasks; monitor workers; document out-of-scope requests.
Perform only tasks in the service plan and approved by the task matrix; decline and report out-of-scope requests; observe and report changes.
Give the list of services and scope of work to clients before contracting, with the contract and whenever it changes.

documentation: Current scope of services (dated, version-controlled) and copy in the IDPH licensing file
Task matrix referencing 245.40(c)(4)
Record of the services list given to each client and each change
Training and competency evaluation records for limited tasks (PER-04, PER-06)
Health care professional's orders where required
Out-of-scope request and referral documentation
Supervisory visit findings

policies.title: Client Acceptance, Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Agency Manager, supervisors and intake staff who receive referrals, accept clients, conduct assessments or discharge clients.
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] decides whom it can safely serve, gathers the information needed to plan care, and routes clients to the correct payer, and to provide the written acceptance and discharge policy required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d).
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item '245.210 d)': initial applicants only, the acceptance of client policy; home services agencies shall develop and follow policies on acceptance and discharge of clients (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d)). [AGENCY NAME] accepts a client based on the client's need for non-medical help, and does not provide medical services. Acceptance is based on documented functional limitations and relevant circumstances, including basic information on medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status. A client who is totally dependent for repositioning is accepted only if the assigned worker is trained and competency-evaluated for that task and the client's representative can assist or give feedback. No one is refused service on the basis of the protected classes listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) (CR-05). Discharge follows this policy and SVC-12: at least 7 working days' written notice with a stated reason, kept in the record, except when worker safety is at risk, in which case the risk is documented. The agency serves clients who pay privately or by private insurance, and Medicaid clients who are served through the IDoA Community Care Program (CCP) or the DHS Division of Rehabilitation Services Home Services Program (HSP).

definitions.definition: The agency's documented decision, after intake and assessment, that it can meet the client's non-medical needs within its scope and has the staff to do so.
Personal information, emergency notification information, agreed service plans, the home services contract, and documentation of services at each visit (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.20).
A client who cannot reposition without help from another person. See SVC-07.
The IDoA-designated entity that assesses CCP participants and refers them to in-home providers.

procedures: Intake staff record each inquiry on the intake log: date, caller, the client's name and address, the client's phone, the person to contact, the payer source, the services requested, and the language and communication needs (CR-05).

Intake staff identify the payer. Private-pay and private-insurance clients are accepted under this policy and CR-06. CCP clients are accepted on referral from the Care Coordination Unit and HSP clients on referral from DHS-DRS, and the agency follows SVC-13 for authorization, rates and reporting. The agency does not accept Medicaid clients outside these programs.
Before accepting a client, the Agency Manager or a supervisor makes an assessment visit at the client's residence, with the client, the representative or POA and, if the client wishes, family.

At the assessment, the assessor documents the client's identifying and emergency notification information, the client's functional limitations and relevant circumstances, and basic information on medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status, including whether the client has dementia (SVC-08).
The assessor documents the services the client needs, the hours and days requested, equipment in the home, hazards to the client or worker (SAF-06), and what the client or family can do.

The assessor determines whether the client's needs are non-medical and within the agency's scope of services (SVC-01). If the client needs services that require a Nurse Practice Act licensee, the agency does not accept the client for those services and refers the client to an appropriate licensed provider.

If the client is totally dependent for repositioning, the Agency Manager accepts the client only if a worker is available who has been trained in the method and passed the agency competency evaluation (PER-04), and the representative can assist or give feedback. The Agency Manager documents these conditions (SVC-07).

The Agency Manager confirms that the agency has qualified, available staff to cover the hours requested and the service area (GOV-02). If it does not, the agency tells the client promptly and offers help finding another provider.

The Agency Manager makes the acceptance decision, signs and dates it, and records the reasons. The decision is based only on need, scope, safety and staffing, and never on a protected class (CR-05). The Administrator reviews every declined referral.

If the agency declines, the Agency Manager informs the client or representative promptly, explains the reason, and gives the names of other resources, for example the Illinois Department on Aging Senior HelpLine at 1-800-252-8966. The reason is documented on the intake log.
If accepted, the Agency Manager provides the services list, rights and responsibilities, privacy notice and complaint information, and signs the client agreement (CR-06) before the first visit.
The Agency Manager develops the service plan with the client and representative before services start (SVC-03) and opens the client record (REC-01).

The agency discharges a client only for a documented reason, such as the client no longer needs home services, the needs exceed the agency's scope, the client or the representative requests it, the payer ends authorization, repeated non-payment, or the client's circumstances create a risk to worker safety.

For a discharge by the agency, the Agency Manager gives the client or representative at least 7 working days' written notice, stating the reason, and keeps a copy in the client record. The 7-day notice does not apply when worker safety is at risk. In that case the Agency Manager documents the risk and notifies the client and any payer as soon as possible (SVC-12).
The Agency Manager helps with transfer by giving the client information on other providers, and, for CCP or HSP clients, notifies the CCU or DHS-DRS counselor (SVC-13).
The Quality Improvement Program reviews acceptance and discharge decisions, including declined referrals, at least annually (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy, reviews declined referrals and discharges, and ensures acceptance decisions follow it.
Conducts or supervises assessments, makes and documents acceptance decisions, issues discharge notices and arranges transition.
Log inquiries, identify the payer and language needs, and schedule assessments.
Conduct assessments as assigned and report hazards and changes.

documentation: Intake log with referral source, payer and reason for any declined referral
Assessment documenting functional limitations, medications, treatments, activity, diet and mental status
Signed acceptance decision with reasons
Documentation that totally dependent repositioning conditions are met
Client agreement and service plan in the client record
Written discharge notice with reason, or documented worker-safety risk
Transition and payer notifications

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Agency Manager, supervisors, caregivers, and clients and their representatives, for every client of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has a written service plan, built with the client, that tells caregivers exactly what to do, stays within the permitted worker scope, and is reviewed and revised as needs change.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item '245.210 e)': initial applicants only, the sample service plan form (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(e)). [AGENCY NAME] writes a service plan for every client, developed with agency staff, the client or representative or POA, and family if the client wishes. The plan covers ADL and in-home support, medication reminders (frequency and time of day), treatments being received, activity, diet, functional limitations and essential procedures, mental health status, frequency of visits, equipment, and client limitations. The plan may not include tasks outside the worker scope in 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4). No physician signature is required. The agency reviews and revises the plan as needed, and at least annually. The agreed service plan is part of the client record (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.20). The agency's sample service plan form is attached to the application and to the client agreement (CR-06).

definitions.definition: The written plan, agreed with the client or representative, that sets out the services, tasks, schedule and client-specific information that workers follow.
The specific steps a worker must follow for a task because of the client's functional limitations, for example how the client needs to be positioned or assisted.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as a guardian or an agent under a power of attorney.

procedures: The Administrator approves a sample service plan form with fields for every required content item: ADL and in-home support; medication reminders with frequency and time of day; treatments being received; activity; diet; functional limitations and essential procedures; mental health status; frequency of visits; equipment; and client limitations. The form is submitted with the IDPH application.

After the assessment (SVC-02) and before the first visit, the Agency Manager develops the plan with the client or representative or POA, and with family if the client wishes. Participants are listed on the plan.
The Agency Manager fills in each field from the assessment and from what the client says he or she wants. Where a field does not apply, it is marked 'none' so that it is clear it was considered.
For ADLs and in-home support, the plan lists each task, the days and times, and any essential procedure or client preference, for example how the client wants to be assisted with bathing.

For medication reminders, the plan lists who pre-selected the medications and the container used, the frequency and the time of day the reminder is given, as limited by SVC-06. The plan does not include medication setup.

For treatments, activity and diet, the plan records what the client is receiving or following, so the worker can support it, for example a prescribed diet or a therapy exercise program. The worker does not perform treatments that require a Nurse Practice Act licensee (SVC-01).

The plan records functional limitations, mental health status, dementia diagnosis or memory problems if known, visit frequency, equipment in the home (for example walker, wheelchair, lift or oxygen), and client limitations such as vision, hearing, language or fall risk.

The Agency Manager checks the plan against the task matrix in SVC-01 and removes any task outside the worker scope in 245.40(c)(4). For any limited task, the Agency Manager confirms client or representative feedback is recorded, the assigned worker is trained and competency-evaluated, and a health care professional's order is on file when required.

The plan does not require a physician's signature. The client or representative, and the Agency Manager, sign and date it. The client receives a copy, and the plan is filed in the client record (REC-01).

Before a caregiver's first visit, the supervisor gives the caregiver the current plan, reviews it with the caregiver, and answers questions. Caregivers follow the plan and do not add or drop tasks without supervisor approval.

The Agency Manager reviews the plan at least annually, and sooner when the client's condition changes, after a hospitalization or fall, when the client or family asks, after a significant incident, or when supervisory visits show the plan does not fit (SVC-04, SVC-11).

Each time the plan is revised, the Agency Manager reviews it with the client or representative, obtains a signature, gives a copy to the client and to the caregivers, and files the superseded plan with the date it was replaced.
If the client's needs change in a way that cannot be met within the agency's scope, the Agency Manager follows SVC-02 and SVC-12.
For CCP and HSP clients, the Agency Manager also checks that the plan is consistent with the program authorization and notifies the program of changes as required (SVC-13).
The Quality Improvement Program audits a sample of service plans at least annually for completeness, scope compliance and timely review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the sample form and ensures it contains every required element.
Develops, signs, reviews and revises each plan with the client, and ensures the plan stays within the permitted scope.
Review the plan with caregivers, check plan compliance during supervisory visits, and report needed changes.
Follow the plan, report changes in the client's condition, and do not perform tasks that are not on the plan.
Take part in developing the plan, tell the agency about changes, and sign the plan.

documentation: Sample service plan form (submitted with the IDPH application)
Signed and dated service plan for each client in the client record
Record of participants in plan development
Dates of plan review and each revision, with superseded plans retained
Competency, training and order records for limited tasks
Annual QI service plan audit

policies.title: Supervisory Visits for Clients
policies.applies_to: All clients receiving in-home services from [AGENCY NAME], and all supervisors, schedulers and home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure every client's care is checked by a qualified supervisor on a regular schedule, that areas of concern lead to an on-site visit, and that a supervisor is always available to workers. Supervisory visits are how [AGENCY NAME] confirms that services match the service plan and that clients are safe and satisfied.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104 item 245.40 c) 6 B) — Supervisory visit for client policy (initial applicants), and implements 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(6). [AGENCY NAME] designates a supervisor who is available to workers for questions at all times. The designated supervisor must meet the qualifications in PER-06. Each client receives routine supervisory visits at least every 90 days. The agency sets this interval as its own minimum standard. The Administrator will shorten it if the full text of 245.40(c)(6)(B), the client's service plan or a payer requires. Whenever a supervisor or any other staff member notes an area of concern, an on-site visit to the client's home is made no later than the next supervisory visit. It is made sooner when the concern involves client safety. The Administrator (agency manager) is responsible for this policy under 245.40(a). Supervisory visits are documented in the client record.

definitions.definition: A planned contact by a qualified supervisor with the client or representative to review the care being given, the service plan, the client's condition and the client's satisfaction.

Any observation, complaint or report suggesting the client may be at risk or not receiving services as planned. Examples are a change in condition, a missed or late visit pattern, a complaint about a worker, a safety hazard, a task done outside the service plan, or a client or family statement of dissatisfaction.
The person named in writing by the Administrator who oversees workers and is available to them for questions at all times.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, such as a power of attorney agent or guardian.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator or designated supervisor enters the client's first supervisory visit due date in the supervision tracking log. The due date is no more than 90 days after the start of services.
The designated supervisor schedules each routine visit with the client or representative at least 5 days ahead when possible, and records the date and time in the tracking log.

During each visit the supervisor reviews the current service plan (SVC-03) with the client or representative. The supervisor checks that tasks match the plan and that no task outside the allowed worker scope (SVC-01) is being done.
The supervisor asks the client or representative about satisfaction with the worker and the schedule, any missed or late visits, and any concerns about safety, privacy, property or treatment.
The supervisor observes the home environment for hazards and checks any equipment named in the service plan.
The supervisor notes any change in the client's condition, functional status or mental status. Changes are handled under SVC-11, and the service plan is updated under SVC-03 when needed.
If the client reports or the supervisor suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation, the supervisor follows SAF-01 immediately and does not wait for the next visit cycle.
If a client raises a complaint, the supervisor tells the client how to file a grievance and starts CR-02.
If an area of concern is noted at any point, the supervisor documents it the same day and tells the Administrator within one business day.

The supervisor schedules an on-site visit to address the concern no later than the next supervisory visit. When there is an immediate risk to the client, the supervisor goes on-site or arranges emergency help that same day.
After a concern-driven visit, the supervisor documents the finding, the action taken (retraining, schedule change, plan revision, referral) and the date the issue was resolved.
The designated supervisor is reachable by workers by phone at all times, including after hours, through [PHONE]. Each worker is given this number in writing at hire.
The Administrator reviews the tracking log monthly. Any visit that is overdue is completed within 7 days, and the cause is recorded.
The supervisor files the signed visit note in the client record (REC-01). Supervisory visit results and overdue visits are reported to the QI program (GOV-04).
The Administrator reviews this policy annually under GOV-03 and confirms the visit interval against the full text of 245.40(c)(6)(B).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the supervisor in writing, ensures supervisor availability at all times, reviews the tracking log monthly and confirms the visit interval against the rule text.
Schedules and completes visits, documents findings, performs on-site visits for areas of concern, and answers worker questions at all times.
Alerts the supervisor to missed-visit patterns and complaints, and keeps the tracking log current.
Reports concerns about a client to the supervisor promptly and cooperates with supervisory visits.

documentation: Supervision tracking log with due and completed dates
Signed supervisory visit note in the client record
Area-of-concern notes and follow-up on-site visit records
Written designation of supervisor and after-hours contact number
Monthly Administrator review notes

policies.title: Supervisory Visits and Annual Observation of Home Services Workers
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and trainers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each home services worker is supervised, observed giving care at least once a year, and supported with follow-up when problems are found.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104 item 245.40 c) 6 B i - iii) — Supervisory visit for home service worker policy (initial applicants), and implements 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(6). The supervisor makes an on-site visit at least once every year to observe and assess each worker giving care in a client's home. When a supervisory visit notes an area of concern about a worker, an on-site visit is made no later than the next supervisory visit. A supervisor or trainer must either (1) have at least 2 years of qualifying experience within the last 5 years, or (2) hold a current supervisory or trainer position and have had training within the past year on the permitted tasks, given or developed by a qualified professional (245.71(g)). Supervisors and trainers are available to workers for continuing education. Each visit and its follow-up is documented. The Administrator will review the full text of 245.40(c)(6)(B)(i)-(iii) when adopting this policy and will update the content of the visit if the rule requires more.

definitions.definition: A visit by a qualified supervisor to the client's home to watch the worker give care and assess the worker's performance against the service plan and training.
Experience that meets the supervisor and trainer requirement in 245.71(g), as verified under PER-06.
Retraining, coaching, re-evaluation of competency or other action taken after an observation shows a deficiency.

procedures: At hire, the Administrator enters each worker's annual observation due date in the supervision tracking log. The due date falls within 12 months of the first assignment and each later anniversary of the last observation.

Only a supervisor or trainer whose qualifications are documented under PER-06 performs observations. The Administrator verifies the 2-years-in-5 experience, or the current-position-plus-training alternative, before the person starts supervising.
The supervisor obtains the client's or representative's permission to observe care in the home and schedules the visit around the worker's regular assignment.

During the visit the supervisor observes the worker giving care and compares it to the client's service plan (SVC-03), including how the worker performs each assigned personal care task and medication reminder (SVC-06, SVC-07).

The supervisor assesses use of infection-control practices, body mechanics and safety (SAF-04, SAF-06), respect for client rights and privacy (CR-01, CR-03), and accurate visit documentation (REC-04).
The supervisor checks that the worker stays within the permitted task scope (SVC-01) and with oxygen-related and dementia care guidance when the client's plan includes them.
The supervisor speaks with the client or representative privately about the worker's care and conduct.
The supervisor completes the observation form the same day. The form records the worker's name, client, date, time, tasks observed, strengths, deficiencies and the supervisor's signature.
The supervisor reviews findings with the worker within 5 business days and both sign the form. The worker may add comments.

When a deficiency is found, the supervisor writes a corrective follow-up plan with a due date. It may include retraining or a repeat competency evaluation (PER-04) before the worker continues the task.
When an area of concern about the worker is noted at any time, the supervisor makes an on-site visit no later than the next supervisory visit. Concerns about client safety are addressed the same day.
Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation seen during an observation is reported under SAF-01 immediately.
The supervisor files the observation and follow-up in the worker's personnel record (PER-11). Training given as a result is recorded under PER-06.
The Administrator reviews the tracking log monthly. Overdue observations are completed within 14 days.
The Administrator uses observation results in annual performance evaluations (PER-12) and in the QI program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures qualified supervisors are in place, tracks due dates monthly and approves corrective plans.
Completes annual observations, documents results, delivers feedback and follow-up, and is available to workers for continuing education.
Participates in the observation, completes any corrective follow-up and signs the observation form.

documentation: Supervision tracking log
Annual observation form signed by supervisor and worker
Corrective follow-up plans and completion records
Supervisor and trainer qualification records (see PER-06)
Entry in the personnel record

policies.title: Medication Reminding and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and schedulers serving clients who take medication
policies.purpose: To define the narrow role of home services workers in medication reminding and to prevent medication setup or administration by non-licensed staff.
policies.policy: A [AGENCY NAME] worker may only remind a client about medications. Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4)(N), the medications must have been pre-selected by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist, and be in containers other than prescription bottles, such as medication minders. Under 245.40(c)(5)(D), workers may not perform or provide medication setup. The client's service plan states the frequency and time of day of reminders (245.210(e)-(g)). Medication reminding is a required training topic (245.71(e)), and a worker must pass a competency evaluation before performing it. As a matter of agency practice, workers do not give, hand, open, crush, mix, measure or place medication, and do not give advice on dosage or on whether to take a medication. The Administrator will confirm the exact wording of the subsections in the full rule text when adopting this policy.

definitions.definition: Verbally prompting a client to take medications at the time listed in the service plan, from medications that are pre-selected and in an allowed container.
Filling or arranging medications in a medication minder or other container, or otherwise preparing doses. Workers may not do this.
A container with compartments for days or times of day, filled by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist.
Chosen and placed in the container by the client, a family member, a nurse or a pharmacist before the worker arrives.

procedures: At assessment (SVC-02), the intake staff member records the client's medication routine, who sets up the medications, and the type of container used.
