The assessor confirms who fills the container (client, family member, nurse or pharmacist) and records that person's name. If no one is able to fill the container, the agency does not accept medication reminding as a service and refers the client to a nurse, pharmacist or other resource.
The service plan (SVC-03) lists medication reminding as a service, with the frequency and time of day of each reminder. It does not list any setup or administration task.
Before a worker's first assignment to a client who needs reminders, the worker completes the required training and passes the competency evaluation on medication reminding (PER-03, PER-04).
At each reminder time the worker checks that medications are in a medication minder or other allowed container and not in a prescription bottle. The worker then gives a verbal reminder.
The client takes the medication by their own action. The worker does not hand the medication to the client, open compartments or put pills in the client's mouth, and does not advise on dose.

If the container is empty, mixed up, shows a missed dose or looks wrong, the worker does not fill or fix it. The worker calls the supervisor at once. The supervisor tells the client or representative and the person who fills the container (family member, nurse or pharmacist).

If medications are only in prescription bottles, the worker does not remind from the bottle. The worker notifies the supervisor, who contacts the client or representative to arrange for a nurse, pharmacist or family member to fill a medication minder.
If the client refuses a medication, the worker does not insist. The worker records the refusal and tells the supervisor the same day.
If the client seems ill or has an apparent reaction, the worker follows SVC-11 and calls 911 for an emergency.
The worker records the reminder time, the client's response and any refusal on the visit record (REC-04).
If a worker is asked by anyone to do medication setup or administration, the worker declines and tells the supervisor. The supervisor explains the limit to the client or family.
The supervisor reviews medication reminding during supervisory visits (SVC-04, SVC-05) and takes corrective action under PER-04 if a worker exceeds scope.
Medication reminding is included in orientation and in annual training (PER-03, PER-05), and any event where a worker went beyond the permitted scope is reported under SAF-03.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy matches the full rule text, ensures workers are trained and evaluated, and reviews scope-of-practice incidents.
Documents who fills the container and sets reminder frequency and time in the service plan.
Responds to worker calls about medication problems, notifies the client or representative, and checks reminding practice at visits.
Gives verbal reminders only, never performs setup or administration, and documents and reports refusals and problems.

documentation: Medication information and container type in the assessment
Service plan entry with frequency and time of day
Competency evaluation record for medication reminding
Visit record entries for reminders and refusals
Incident reports for scope exceedance or medication concerns

policies.title: Personal Care Task Limits, Positioning and Oxygen-Related Support
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and trainers who assign, teach or perform personal care tasks
policies.purpose: To make sure personal care tasks are performed only within the limits set by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c)(4), by trained and evaluated workers, and with the client input and professional orders the rule requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] workers perform only the personal care tasks permitted under 245.40(c)(4). These tasks include skin care, ambulation, bathing, dressing and compression garments, exercise, feeding and thickener, hair care, mouth care, nail care, positioning, shaving and toileting, and other listed tasks. For most tasks, the agency obtains feedback from the client or representative on how the task is to be done, the worker is trained in the method, and the agency completes a competency evaluation before the worker does the task. Some tasks also require an order from a health care professional. The agency obtains the order and files it in the client record before assigning the task. Workers do not perform passive range of motion, do not trim nails, and do not provide skilled skin care. The service plan may not include any task outside this scope (245.210(e)-(g)). No assignment is made until the worker passes the competency evaluation (245.71(c)). Annual training includes oxygen delivery for workers who serve clients on oxygen (245.71(f)). The Administrator will read the full text of 245.40(c)(4), including items after toileting, and apply any added limits.

definitions.definition: A written or documented order from a licensed health care professional authorized to give it, for a task that the rule says requires one.
An observed demonstration and test by a qualified supervisor or trainer showing that the worker can safely perform a task.
Helping a client change or maintain body position (for example in bed or chair) within the limits of 245.40(c)(4) and the training received.
Support for a client who uses oxygen, limited to what the worker was trained to do and the service plan allows, such as keeping tubing clear and following safety precautions.
Care that requires a nurse's skills, such as wound treatment or dressing changes. Workers may not perform it.

procedures: At assessment (SVC-02), the supervisor identifies every personal care task the client needs and compares each with the list in 245.40(c)(4). Tasks outside the list are not accepted. The client or representative is told which tasks the agency cannot provide, and referral options are offered.
For each accepted task the supervisor asks the client or representative how the task should be done and records the feedback in the assessment and service plan.

The supervisor checks whether the task requires a health care professional's order. If so, the order is obtained from the client's professional before the task is assigned, and a copy is filed in the client record (REC-01).
The supervisor writes the service plan (SVC-03) listing only permitted tasks, with the client's stated preferences and any order. The plan is reviewed with the client or representative.

Before a worker's first assignment, the worker completes the first 5 hours of initial training and passes the competency evaluation (PER-03, PER-04). The worker is evaluated again after the remaining 5 hours.

Before a worker performs a task requiring a specific method, such as positioning, bathing, toileting or feeding with thickener, the worker is trained in that method and passes a competency evaluation on it.
Schedulers assign workers only if their records show evaluation on all tasks in the client's plan (SVC-09).
Workers do not perform passive range-of-motion exercise, trim nails or give skilled skin care. If asked, the worker declines politely and tells the supervisor.

Positioning is done only in the manner taught, with the client's input. Workers do not use techniques or devices they have not been trained on. If a client cannot be moved safely, the worker stops and calls the supervisor. The worker calls 911 if there is an emergency (SVC-11).

For clients who use oxygen, workers who serve them complete oxygen delivery training annually (PER-05). Workers follow the service plan and the client's safety rules, such as no smoking or open flame near oxygen.

Workers do not change oxygen flow settings. If the client appears short of breath, the equipment looks faulty or the supply is low, the worker calls the supervisor. The worker calls 911 if the client is in distress.
The worker records each task performed on the visit record (REC-04), and any refusal or difficulty.
The supervisor reviews task performance at supervisory visits (SVC-04, SVC-05). When a change in client condition affects a task, the plan is updated and any new order is obtained.
Tasks performed outside scope, or injuries during care, are reported under SAF-03, and the Administrator decides on retraining.
Annual training must include the ADL tasks in 245.40(c)(4) (PER-05), and the Administrator reviews the training content each year.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the task list matches the full rule text, ensures workers are evaluated and orders obtained, and reviews scope incidents.
Assesses needs, gathers client feedback, obtains orders, trains and evaluates workers, and updates plans.
Assigns only workers with documented competency on the client's tasks.
Performs only trained, permitted and planned tasks, refuses prohibited tasks, and reports concerns.

documentation: Client or representative feedback in assessment and service plan
Health care professional orders in the client record
Competency evaluation records by task
Annual oxygen delivery training record for applicable workers
Visit records and incident reports

policies.title: Dementia Care and Related Training
policies.applies_to: All home services workers, supervisors and trainers; all clients with dementia or memory loss
policies.purpose: To make sure workers assigned to clients with dementia are trained to communicate with them, understand dementia and respond to challenging behaviors safely and respectfully.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] trains every worker on understanding dementia, problem-solving for challenging dementia behaviors, and communication with people who have dementia or are hard of hearing, as required in the initial training subjects of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e). No worker is assigned to a client with dementia until this training is completed and documented. The Administrator will also verify, from the full text of the Illinois rules and IDPH survey guidance, any added dementia training that applies, including required hours, and add it to the curriculum. Dementia training is documented for each worker assigned to a client with dementia (see PER-06). Care of clients with dementia is based on dignity, safety, individual preferences and the client's own service plan.

definitions.definition: A condition that causes loss of memory, thinking and the ability to carry out daily activities, such as Alzheimer's disease.
Behavior such as agitation, wandering, repeated questions, resistance to care, or aggression that can arise from dementia and that requires a calm, planned response.
Speaking in simple, calm, respectful terms and adjusting approach to the client's abilities and history.

procedures: During assessment (SVC-02), the assessor records any diagnosis or signs of dementia or memory loss, wandering risk, behavior patterns, triggers and calming strategies, using information from the client, representative, family and referral source.

The service plan (SVC-03) states the client's functional and mental status, safety needs, preferred routines and the approach that works for challenging behavior. It is shared with every assigned worker.

Initial training (PER-03) includes understanding dementia, problem-solving for challenging dementia behaviors, and communication with people who have dementia or are hard of hearing, as required by 245.71(e).

The trainer covers topics such as approach and tone, redirection, routines, avoiding arguments, safe responses to resistance during bathing or dressing, wandering prevention and when to call for help.
The trainer meets the qualifications in PER-06, and training content is reviewed by the Administrator at least annually.
The Administrator verifies and adds any further dementia training required by Illinois rule or IDPH guidance, including the number of hours, and records the requirement in the training plan.
A worker must complete dementia training and pass the competency evaluation before being assigned to a dementia client. Schedulers check the training record before each assignment (SVC-09).

The worker follows the client's plan and uses calm, non-confrontational methods. The worker does not use restraint, force, threats or punishment. If safety cannot be maintained, the worker leaves the client in a safe place and calls the supervisor, or calls 911 in an emergency.

If a client with dementia may have wandered or left the home, the worker calls 911 and then the supervisor immediately. The agency notifies the family or representative and files an incident report (SAF-03).
A new or worsening behavior is reported to the supervisor the same day. The supervisor reviews the client, notifies the representative and updates the plan (SVC-03, SVC-11).
Workers watch for signs of abuse, neglect or exploitation, because clients with dementia may not be able to report them. All concerns are reported under SAF-01.
The supervisor reviews dementia care during supervisory visits and annual observations (SVC-04, SVC-05).
Dementia training is documented with date, minutes per topic, instructor and qualifications, content description and worker signature (PER-06), and filed in the personnel record (PER-11).
Dementia-related training is repeated or refreshed when a worker shows a need, and the Administrator includes dementia topics in annual training planning (PER-05).

responsibilities.duty: Verifies full dementia training requirements, approves curriculum, and makes sure only trained workers are assigned.
Delivers or arranges training, shares client-specific approaches and monitors care.
Checks dementia training records before assigning a worker to a client with dementia.
Completes training, uses person-centered approaches, and reports behavior changes, wandering and safety concerns.

documentation: Dementia and behavior information in the assessment and service plan
Dementia training records with date, minutes per topic, instructor and signature
Competency evaluation records
Incident reports for wandering or behavior events
Annual training plan

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Schedulers, supervisors, the Administrator and all home services workers
policies.purpose: To make sure each client receives the visits in the service plan from qualified workers, that missed visits are handled promptly, and that clients can reach the agency outside business hours.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules visits to match the frequency of visits in the client's service plan (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(e)-(g)). Only workers who have passed the required competency evaluation and have completed background checks are assigned to clients (PER-02, PER-04). The agency's operating-hours policy tells clients how to reach the agency outside operating hours (245.40(a); GOV-08). Illinois rules do not set a missed-visit timeframe, so the agency sets its own standards. The agency tells the client or representative of a missed or changed visit within 30 minutes of learning of it, and arranges replacement coverage or an alternate plan as described below. Clients are told of this standard in the service agreement (CR-06).

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that did not start within 30 minutes of the scheduled time and for which the client was not told of a change in advance.
Assigning another qualified worker to the visit, or an agreed alternative time.
Keeping the same workers where possible, sharing the service plan with replacements, and avoiding gaps in care.
A worker who has completed background checks, required training and a competency evaluation on the tasks in the client's plan.

procedures: After the service plan is completed (SVC-03), the scheduler creates the schedule to match the visit days, times and length in the plan, and confirms it with the client or representative.

Before each assignment the scheduler checks that the worker has a cleared background check and registry check (PER-02), has finished the required initial training and passed the competency evaluation (PER-03, PER-04), and has the tasks and dementia training the client's plan requires (SVC-07, SVC-08).
The scheduler gives the worker the client's address, schedule and a copy of, or access to, the service plan before the first visit.
Where possible, the scheduler assigns a consistent primary worker and a named back-up worker for each client.
Clients are given the office phone [PHONE], the hours of operation, and the after-hours number and instructions in writing at admission, in line with GOV-08.

A worker who cannot attend a visit calls the office as soon as the need is known and no later than 2 hours before the start time, except in emergencies. Workers do not make their own arrangements with the client or other workers.
If a worker has not checked in (SVC-10) within 30 minutes of the start time, the scheduler calls the worker and then the client or representative.
When a visit is missed or the worker will not be available, the scheduler or on-call supervisor notifies the client or representative within 30 minutes and offers replacement coverage.

The scheduler offers a qualified replacement first. If none is available, the supervisor offers a different time on the same day, and may ask the client's family or other supports to help temporarily.

If the client is at risk without the visit, the supervisor contacts the client directly. If the client cannot be reached and risk is suspected, the supervisor asks for a welfare check by calling 911 or another local emergency number as needed (SVC-11).
The scheduler records each missed or changed visit, the reason, the time the client was notified and the replacement arranged on the visit schedule log, and tells the supervisor.
A visit that cannot be made up is reported to the supervisor, who documents it. The supervisor considers whether the service plan needs revision and whether a payer must be notified (SVC-13).
The supervisor reviews patterns of missed visits, late arrivals or worker turnover for each client, and makes an on-site visit if there is an area of concern (SVC-04).
When a worker is replaced for any reason, the supervisor tells the client, reviews the service plan with the new worker, and documents the handoff.
The Administrator reviews missed-visit data each month in the QI program (GOV-04), and acts on repeated problems.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures sufficient qualified staff, approves the missed-visit standards, and reviews monthly data.
Builds schedules from service plans, checks worker qualifications, finds replacements and logs missed visits.
Handles missed visits and client contact, including after hours, and reviews plans and patterns.
Arrives on time, calls early if unable to attend, and does not leave a client without notice.

documentation: Client schedules matching the service plan
Worker qualification checks before assignment
Missed-visit and replacement log with times of client notification
On-call and after-hours contact records
Monthly missed-visit data reviewed in the QI program

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, scheduling staff, supervisors, billing staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every visit is verified and documented accurately, that Medicaid-funded personal care visits meet Illinois Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) requirements, and that every visit, whatever the payer, is documented in the client record.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] documents every visit with the caregiver, client, service, time in, time out and location. For any Medicaid-funded personal care visit, [AGENCY NAME] captures this information through an electronic visit verification system as required by 42 USC 1396b(l) and Illinois HFS EVV policy. Illinois integrates personal care EVV data in HHAeXchange from March 2, 2026. HFS requires at least 75% quarterly EVV compliance from April 1, 2026. The state EVV solution is offered to providers at no cost, and [AGENCY NAME] will evaluate and use it before purchasing a paid system. [AGENCY NAME] serves Medicaid clients only through the IDoA Community Care Program or DHS-DRS Home Services Program, as described in SVC-13. Private-pay and private-insurance visits are not required to use state EVV. They are still documented at each visit as part of the client record, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.20 and 245.210(h). The agency applies the same timekeeping standards to all visits so payroll, billing and client records agree.

definitions.definition: An electronic system that records the caregiver, client, service, time in, time out and GPS location of a visit as the visit happens.
The percentage of Medicaid-funded visits in a quarter that have complete, system-captured EVV data without manual edits. The agency tracks this against the HFS minimum of 75% per quarter.
A correction to EVV data made after the visit, such as a missed clock-in or clock-out. It requires a reason code and supervisor approval.
As defined in 245.20: personal information, emergency notification information, agreed service plans, the home services contract, and documentation of services at each visit.

procedures: The Administrator designates an EVV Coordinator ([EVV COORDINATOR NAME]) before the agency accepts its first Medicaid-funded client. This person is responsible for system setup, user accounts, reporting and the compliance reviews in this policy.

Before serving any Medicaid-funded client, the Administrator confirms with IDoA or DHS-DRS (as applicable) which EVV system and data-exchange process the program requires, and records the answer in the agency's payer file. The Administrator also confirms that the agency can send data to HHAeXchange or use the state EVV solution.
The EVV Coordinator evaluates the free state EVV solution first. If the agency chooses another system, the Administrator documents the reason and confirms the system can integrate with HHAeXchange.

The EVV system is configured to capture, for every visit: caregiver, client, service performed, time in, time out and GPS location. The EVV Coordinator tests this setup before go-live and documents the test.
The EVV Coordinator creates a separate login for each caregiver and gives the caregiver written instructions. Caregivers may never share logins or clock in or out for another person.

Training on EVV is part of orientation. The trainer demonstrates clock-in, clock-out, service entry and what to do if the device fails. The caregiver's training record shows completion before the first Medicaid-funded visit.

At the start of every visit, the caregiver clocks in at the client's home using the EVV system. At the end, the caregiver clocks out and selects the services provided. The caregiver does not clock in before arriving or clock out after leaving.

If the system fails or the caregiver cannot clock in, the caregiver calls the office or on-call supervisor at [PHONE] during the visit and records the actual start time, end time and reason. The supervisor logs the call.

Manual edits are made only by the scheduler or EVV Coordinator, only with a reason code, and only after the supervisor confirms the actual visit times with the caregiver. The edit, reason and approver are recorded in the system audit trail. Caregivers may not edit their own visits.

The scheduler reviews the EVV exception report daily (each business day) for missed clock-ins, missed clock-outs, visits without GPS and visits that do not match the schedule. Exceptions are resolved within 2 business days where possible.

Each caregiver completes the documentation of services for every visit, whatever the payer, as required by REC-04. For private-pay visits the documentation shows date, time in, time out and services performed, and is filed in the client record under 245.210(h).
Billing staff do not submit a Medicaid claim for a visit unless the EVV record matches the services and times authorized under the client's service plan and the payer's authorization.

The EVV Coordinator calculates the EVV compliance rate each month and reports it to the Administrator. The agency's internal target is 90%. If the monthly rate falls below 85%, or any quarterly rate falls below 75%, the Administrator opens a corrective action, identifies causes and retrains the staff involved.
Payroll uses verified visit times, and any unpaid or paid travel is handled under PER-15. Time that differs from the schedule is reviewed with the caregiver before payroll closes.

Caregivers who falsify time, clock in or out for someone else, or record services not provided are subject to discipline up to termination. The Administrator reviews the case under GOV-05 (billing integrity) and reports as that policy requires.
EVV reports, manual-edit logs and compliance reviews are included in the quality improvement review under GOV-04 at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms program EVV requirements, designates the EVV Coordinator, reviews compliance rates and approves corrective actions.
Sets up and tests the system, manages accounts, reviews exceptions, tracks compliance and reports monthly.
Reviews daily exceptions, verifies and approves manual edits and handles caregiver system problems.
Clocks in and out personally at the client's home, records services accurately and reports system problems right away.
Bill only visits supported by matching EVV and visit documentation.

documentation: EVV system setup and test records
Caregiver EVV training records
Daily exception reports and resolution notes
Manual-edit audit trail with reason codes and approver
Monthly and quarterly EVV compliance reports and corrective action plans
Visit documentation filed in each client record (REC-04)

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervisors, on-call staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers observe, report and document changes in a client's condition, respond safely to emergencies, and notify the right people on the same day.
policies.policy: Caregivers observe, report and document changes in client functioning, as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c) permits. Caregivers do not diagnose, give medical advice or provide medical treatment. Caregiver training under 245.71(e) covers emergencies, first aid and the client's emergency preparedness plan, and caregivers act within that training. In an emergency the caregiver calls 911 first. The caregiver then notifies the client's representative and the emergency contact listed in the client record, and reports to the supervisor the same day. [AGENCY NAME] updates the service plan when a change in condition affects the services the client needs.

definitions.definition: Any noticeable difference in a client's physical, mental or emotional functioning, behavior, appetite, mobility, safety or home environment compared with what the caregiver normally sees or what the service plan describes.

A situation that threatens life, safety or health and needs immediate help. Examples are unresponsiveness, chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, a serious fall or injury, fire, or a person with a weapon.
The person listed in the client record to be called when the client has an emergency or serious change in condition.

procedures: During orientation under PER-03, the trainer teaches caregivers what to watch for (for example new confusion, falls, skin changes, changes in eating, drinking or toileting, new pain complaints, or signs of abuse or neglect) and how to report them. Competency is checked under PER-04.

Before the first visit, the supervisor makes sure the client record has the representative's contact information and an emergency contact, and that the caregiver knows where to find them in the home and in the office file.
The caregiver reviews the client's emergency preparedness plan (SAF-05) at the first visit and knows the exits, the phone, and the plan for evacuation or sheltering.

If the client is unresponsive, has trouble breathing, chest pain, stroke symptoms, a serious injury, uncontrolled bleeding or any other life-threatening problem, the caregiver calls 911 immediately. The caregiver gives the address, describes what is happening and follows the dispatcher's instructions.

While waiting for help, the caregiver gives only the first aid they were trained to give and stays with the client unless there is danger to the caregiver. If a fall has occurred, the caregiver does not move the client unless there is immediate danger.

The caregiver unlocks the door or arranges access for responders, gathers any medication list or medical information kept in the home and gives it to responders. The caregiver does not give medications or any treatment beyond training.

As soon as the client is safe, the caregiver notifies the office or on-call supervisor at [PHONE] and the supervisor then notifies the client's representative and the emergency contact. If the supervisor cannot reach anyone, the supervisor keeps trying and documents each attempt.

For a non-emergency change in condition, the caregiver tells the client or representative what was noticed and calls the supervisor the same day. The caregiver does not wait for the next supervisory visit.
The supervisor reviews the report the same day, decides whether the representative should contact the client's physician, and records the advice given. The supervisor does not give medical advice.
If a change suggests possible abuse, neglect or exploitation, the caregiver and supervisor follow SAF-01 immediately and, where required, SAF-02.
If the client dies, the caregiver calls 911 and then the supervisor. If the death may not be from disease or natural causes, SAF-02 also applies.
The caregiver writes a factual note in the visit record before leaving or as soon as the emergency allows. It states what was seen, the time, who was called, what was done and who arrived.
The caregiver or supervisor completes an incident report under SAF-03 for any emergency, injury, fall or hospital transfer, within the time set in that policy.
The supervisor contacts the client or representative within 1 business day to check on the client's status and whether services should continue, change or pause.

When a change affects needs or safety, the supervisor schedules a plan review and updates the service plan under SVC-03. If needs now exceed non-medical services, the supervisor starts the process in SVC-12.
The Administrator reviews emergency events at least quarterly as part of the quality improvement program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Observes, reports and documents changes, calls 911 in emergencies, gives only trained first aid and reports to the supervisor the same day.
Takes the report, notifies the representative and emergency contact, follows up within 1 business day and updates the service plan.
Makes sure caregivers are trained and that emergency contacts are in each record. Reviews events for trends.

documentation: Visit note describing the change or emergency
Supervisor's record of calls to the representative, emergency contact and others
Incident report (SAF-03)
Service plan update and plan-review note (SVC-03)
Training records on emergencies, first aid and emergency preparedness (245.71(e))

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, schedulers, intake staff and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure services end only for allowable reasons, with the notice the rule requires, and with a documented plan for the client to move to another provider.
policies.policy: This policy meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item 245.210 d) (written policies on acceptance and discharge of clients; 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(d)). The discharge half is set out here. The acceptance half is in SVC-02. [AGENCY NAME] develops and follows these written discharge policies. [AGENCY NAME] gives a client at least 7 working days' written notice before ending services, states the reason in the notice, and keeps a copy in the client record. The 7-day notice does not apply when a worker's safety is at risk. In that case the risk is documented in the client record. No client is discharged or refused service because of any protected class listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q). [AGENCY NAME] accepts clients based on need for non-medical help and does not provide medical services. Discharge is considered when a client's needs go beyond non-medical services. The agency documents a plan for transfer or referral to another provider for every discharge it initiates.

definitions.definition: Ending all services to a client, whether the client, the agency or a payer initiates it.
Monday through Friday, excluding legal holidays, as counted in the agency's notice.

A situation in which continuing to send a caregiver to the home would expose the caregiver to a reasonable risk of harm, such as threats, violence, sexual harassment, a weapon or an unsafe environment that cannot be corrected.
The characteristics protected under the Illinois Human Rights Act on which service may never be refused or ended.

procedures: Only the Administrator or a designee approves an agency-initiated discharge. A caregiver or scheduler may not end services on their own.

Acceptable reasons for agency-initiated discharge are: the client's needs now require medical services or care the agency cannot provide; a totally dependent client who needs repositioning can no longer be served because the assigned worker is not trained and competency-evaluated, or the representative can no longer assist or give feedback; non-payment after documented attempts to resolve it; the home is unsafe for caregivers and the hazard is not corrected; or the agency is closing or no longer serves the area. Any other reason must be reviewed and approved by the Administrator in writing.
The Administrator confirms the discharge is not based on any protected class listed in 775 ILCS 5/1-103(Q) and records that confirmation in the client record.

Before a non-safety discharge, the supervisor tries to resolve the problem by talking with the client or representative, adjusting the service plan under SVC-03, or training the staff. These efforts are documented.

The Administrator issues a written notice to the client and representative at least 7 working days before the last day of service. The notice states the reason in plain language, the last date of service, the transfer plan and how to contact the agency about concerns (see CR-02). A copy is placed in the client record.

The notice is delivered by [HAND DELIVERY/MAIL/EMAIL AS THE CLIENT CHOSE IN THE SERVICE AGREEMENT]. The supervisor also calls the client or representative to explain it and records the date and time of the call.
Services continue as scheduled during the 7 working days unless the client or representative requests otherwise or a safety risk exists.

If a worker's safety is at risk, the Administrator may end or suspend services right away without 7 working days' notice. The Administrator documents in the record what happened, who was involved, why it posed a risk, and the date and time services stopped. The agency still gives written notice with the reason as soon as possible.
If the safety risk involves possible abuse, neglect or exploitation of the client or by the client, the supervisor also follows SAF-01 and SAF-02.

For every agency-initiated discharge, the supervisor prepares a transfer plan. The plan lists alternative providers or referral sources offered to the client, such as other licensed agencies, the IDoA Senior HelpLine 1-800-252-8966 or the client's Care Coordination Unit, if applicable. It also records what information was shared (with consent, under CR-03) and the date it was given.

For clients served through the IDoA Community Care Program or the DHS-DRS Home Services Program, the supervisor notifies the Care Coordination Unit or DRS counselor as the program requires (see SVC-13) and documents the date.

If the client or representative ends services, the supervisor records the date, who made the request and the reason if given, confirms the last date of service, and offers help with transfer or referral.
If services end because the client is hospitalized, moves into a facility or dies, the supervisor documents the date and circumstances and closes the record without a 7-day notice.

On the last day of service, the supervisor makes sure all client property is returned and the agency's equipment is retrieved, and that the caregiver's final visit note is filed. Final billing is settled under CR-06.
The supervisor completes a discharge summary in the client record within 5 working days after the last date of service. It includes the reason, notice date, transfer plan and any unresolved concerns.
The record is closed and retained as required by REC-01. The Administrator reviews discharges quarterly for trends under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Approves each agency-initiated discharge, confirms no protected-class basis, issues the written notice and documents any safety exception.
Attempts resolution, prepares the transfer plan, communicates with the client, representative and payer, and completes the discharge summary.
Maintains the schedule through the notice period and removes the client from the schedule after the last date of service.
Reports safety concerns immediately and documents the final visit.

documentation: Written discharge notice with stated reason and copy of delivery method
Supervisor's documentation of resolution efforts and calls
Administrator's approval and protected-class review
Documentation of any worker-safety risk that allowed shorter notice
Transfer or referral plan
Discharge summary and closed client record

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers (CCP and HSP)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, intake staff, supervisors, schedulers and billing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] correctly handles private-pay, private-insurance and Medicaid-program clients, and works with IDoA, HFS and DHS-DRS without misrepresenting its licensure or billing improperly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed by IDPH as a home services agency. A licensed agency takes private pay or private insurance. Medicaid clients are served through the IDoA Community Care Program (CCP) or the DHS-DRS Home Services Program (HSP). Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.20, programs serving clients exclusively through IDoA CCP, DHS Office of Rehabilitation Services, or the VA are not home services agencies. [AGENCY NAME] will not accept or bill a Medicaid-funded client until the Administrator has confirmed provider enrollment steps and requirements with IDoA and DRS and documented them. IDoA is the operating agency and HFS is the state Medicaid agency for the Persons who are Elderly waiver. [AGENCY NAME] follows the service authorization, plan of care, rates and requirements of the funding program for any program client. For these clients, service planning respects the client's choices as 42 CFR 441.301(c) requires of home and community-based services.

definitions.definition: The IDoA program, operating under the Persons who are Elderly HCBS waiver, that pays for in-home services for eligible older adults. Care Coordination Units assess and refer clients.
The DHS-DRS program that serves people with severe disabilities under age 60.
The local agency that assesses CCP clients and refers them to in-home providers.
The program's written approval stating the service, hours and dates for which the provider may bill.

procedures: Before the agency accepts any Medicaid-funded client, the Administrator contacts IDoA (and DHS-DRS for HSP) to confirm the provider enrollment steps, agreements and requirements that apply to the agency, and documents the contacts and answers in the payer file. Billing for program clients does not begin until enrollment is confirmed.

The Administrator records for each program the rate, service code, billing requirements and EVV requirements. As of the dates posted by the programs, these are: CCP in-home service (S5130) $30.80 per hour, or $32.57 per hour with insurance, effective 1/1/2026; HSP homemaker (4100) $30.80 per hour, updated 7/1/2026. The Administrator verifies current rates at least every 6 months and whenever a program announces a change.
At first contact, intake staff ask each caller how services will be paid for: private pay, private insurance, CCP or HSP. They record the answer on the intake form under SVC-02.

If the caller may be eligible for CCP, intake staff explain that applications go through the IDoA Senior HelpLine at 1-800-252-8966 and that a CCU assesses and refers clients. If the caller may be eligible for HSP, intake staff direct the caller to DHS-DRS. Intake staff do not promise eligibility, approval or a start date.
For private-pay or private-insurance clients, the agency follows its own rates and service agreement under CR-06, and all other policies in this manual apply.
For a client referred by a CCU or DRS, the supervisor obtains the written service authorization and plan of care before the first visit. Services are limited to what is authorized.
The supervisor prepares the agency's service plan under SVC-03 so that it matches the program's plan, respects the client's preferences and is consistent with SVC-01 (scope of services).
Caregivers for program clients complete visit documentation under REC-04 and EVV under SVC-10 for each visit.

The agency does not bill a program client or family for services the program covers, and does not bill for any hours not authorized, unless the program allows it in writing. Any private-pay hours added beyond authorized hours are covered by a separate signed agreement under CR-06 and are not billed to the program.

The supervisor reports changes in a program client's condition, hospital stays, or other events to the CCU or DRS counselor as the program requires, and documents the date and name of the person notified (see SVC-11).

Billing staff submit claims only for authorized, verified visits, within the program's deadlines, and reconcile payments monthly. Overpayments or errors are corrected and repaid as the program requires (see GOV-05).
The agency cooperates with program monitoring, reviews and audits. The Administrator is the contact for all requests, and records are produced as REC-02 allows.
If the agency discharges a program client, it follows SVC-12 and tells the CCU or DRS counselor so a replacement provider can be arranged.
If program enrollment is denied, suspended or ended, the Administrator tells affected clients and their representatives promptly, documents the notice, and follows SVC-12 for each client.
The Administrator does not state or imply in marketing or client communications that the agency is a Medicaid provider unless enrollment has been confirmed (see GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms enrollment steps and requirements with IDoA and DRS, verifies rates, oversees billing integrity and is the contact for program audits.
Identify the payer source, give accurate referral information and obtain authorizations.
Aligns the service plan with the program plan, reports changes to the CCU or DRS and monitors authorized hours.
Bill only authorized and verified visits and reconcile payments.

documentation: Payer file with enrollment confirmations and program contacts
Rate and requirement reference sheet with verification dates
Service authorizations and program plans of care
Intake payer-source record
Communications with CCU, IDoA, DRS and HFS
Claims, EVV records and payment reconciliations

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors, supervisors and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and financial exploitation of clients and to make sure every reasonable suspicion is reported promptly to the right authority and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of any client. Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250, anyone who has a reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a client aged 60 or older, a client with a disability, or any 'eligible adult' under the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20) must notify the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging. If the victim is under 18, the report goes to the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. Employees and volunteers must report to management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA. Reporting to a supervisor does not replace the report to the outside agency. [AGENCY NAME] documents each report and keeps the documentation on premises for 12 months. Mandated-reporter duties under 320 ILCS 20 remain for every person to whom they apply. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited. Investigation of reports and law enforcement notification are covered in SAF-02.

definitions.definition: Physical, sexual or emotional harm or confinement of a client, as defined in the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20).
Failure to provide, or willful withholding of, the care, food, shelter, medical care or supervision a client needs.
Using a client's money, property or assets improperly or without consent, including by deception or pressure.
An adult covered by the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20).
The agency designated by IDoA to receive and respond to reports. The local Area Agency on Aging may also receive reports.
A belief, based on what a person saw, heard or was told, that abuse, neglect or exploitation may have happened. Proof is not required.

procedures: Prevention: the agency screens every employee through background checks and Health Care Worker Registry checks before client contact (PER-02) and trains every caregiver on abuse and neglect and their reporting duties during orientation (PER-03).

Prevention: supervisors observe caregivers and talk with clients at supervisory visits (SVC-04, SVC-05) and ask clients whether they feel safe and well treated. Observations and concerns are documented.

Prevention: caregivers follow professional boundaries (PER-13) and the rules on client property, gifts and money (CR-04). Caregivers may not borrow from or accept gifts or payment from clients, use client financial accounts, or take part in changes to a client's will or legal documents.

Prevention: new employees receive the agency's written statement of the reporting duty and sign that they received it. The Administrator posts the telephone numbers below in the office and gives them to each caregiver.

Reporting contacts: IDoA Adult Protective Services hotline 1-866-800-1409 [verify current number before adoption]; local elder abuse provider agency [NAME AND PHONE]; local Area Agency on Aging [NAME AND PHONE]; DCFS Child Abuse Hotline 1-800-25-ABUSE (1-800-252-2873) for victims under 18.

Any employee or volunteer who has a reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a client immediately reports it to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA (or to IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging), and also reports to the supervisor or Administrator. The employee makes the outside report without delay, before the end of the shift at the latest, and does not wait for a supervisor's approval.
If the client is under 18, the employee calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline and then notifies the supervisor.

If the client is in immediate danger, or if one of the situations in SAF-02 applies (injury caused by staff, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home, or a death not due to disease or natural causes), the employee calls 911 or local police first, then makes the report required here.

The employee does not question the client in detail, confront the suspected person, or investigate. The employee protects the client's safety, preserves any evidence, and writes down what was seen or heard, the date, the time and the names of any witnesses.
The supervisor or Administrator who receives a report confirms the outside report was made. If it was not, the supervisor or Administrator makes it right away and documents the date and time.

The person who made the report records it on the agency's Abuse/Neglect/Exploitation Report Form on the same day: client, date, what was suspected, who was told, the agency's name, the report date and time, any case number given, and the actions taken.
If the person suspected is an employee, the Administrator removes that employee from direct client contact immediately and starts the investigation under SAF-02.

The Administrator or supervisor tells the client's representative of the report unless doing so would put the client at risk or the representative is the suspected person. The decision and reason are documented.
The Administrator makes sure the client has continued safe care and updates the service plan (SVC-03) or schedule as needed, without punishing the client for the report.

Each report and its documentation are filed in a confidential abuse-report file kept on the premises for at least 12 months. The client record cross-references the report without disclosing more than necessary (see CR-03).
No one may retaliate against an employee or volunteer who reports in good faith. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination (PER-13).
The Administrator reviews all reports at least quarterly under GOV-04 for patterns and training needs, and the topic is part of each caregiver's annual training (PER-05).

responsibilities.duty: Report reasonable suspicion immediately to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA and to management, and write down what they saw.
Confirms the outside report was made, completes the report form, protects the client and informs the Administrator.
Removes employees from client contact when needed, starts investigations, keeps the reports on premises for 12 months and monitors training.

documentation: Abuse/Neglect/Exploitation Report Form for every report
Record of the date, time and agency contacted and any case number
Confidential abuse-report file kept on premises for 12 months
Employee acknowledgment of the reporting duty
Orientation and annual training records on abuse and neglect
Supervisory visit notes on client safety

policies.title: Abuse Investigations and Law Enforcement Notification
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, all employees and contractors
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] protects clients, investigates reports of abuse, neglect or exploitation, reports results to IDPH, and notifies law enforcement.
policies.policy: This is the written law-enforcement notification policy required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250. If an employee is the alleged perpetrator of abuse, neglect or exploitation, [AGENCY NAME] removes the employee from direct client contact immediately and investigates. [AGENCY NAME] completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report. The report is sent to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, and a copy is kept for 12 months. The report contains each of the six elements required by 245.250(d). [AGENCY NAME] calls 911 or local police immediately for staff-inflicted physical injury, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home by another person, or a death other than by disease or natural causes. Reporting under SAF-01 and any mandated-reporter duty under 320 ILCS 20 continue and are never replaced by an internal investigation.

definitions.definition: The person suspected of having caused the abuse, neglect or exploitation.
The first report of the suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the agency's management. The 14-day period starts on the date of this report.
The written report that documents the agency's investigation and contains the six elements required by 245.250(d).
911 or the local police or sheriff's department that has jurisdiction where the client lives.

procedures: Immediate police notification: whoever is on site or first learns of any of the following calls 911 or local police at once: physical injury inflicted by staff; sexual abuse by staff; a crime committed in the home by another person; or a death other than by disease or natural causes. The caller then notifies the supervisor or Administrator.
The person who calls police records the date, time, agency, officer name and any report number, and gives the information to the Administrator the same day.
Staff cooperate with law enforcement. The Administrator is the contact for police inquiries and releases client information only as allowed by CR-03 and REC-02.

When an initial report of abuse, neglect or exploitation names an employee as the alleged perpetrator, the Administrator removes the employee from all direct client contact immediately, before any interview or decision. The Administrator tells the employee in writing and documents the date and time.

The Administrator makes sure the client is safe and that a different caregiver is assigned, with the client's agreement, so services continue. If the Administrator is the alleged perpetrator, the Governing Body designee ([GOVERNING BODY CONTACT]) takes over the investigation.
The Administrator confirms that the report required by SAF-01 was made to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA (or to DCFS for a victim under 18) and cooperates with that agency's investigation.
The Administrator opens an investigation file and sets the dates: the initial report date and the due date (14 days later).

The investigator (the Administrator or a designated person who is not involved in the incident) interviews the client or representative as appropriate, the reporter, any witnesses and the employee, and reviews schedules, EVV and visit records, and other relevant documents. Interviews are conducted privately and documented with the date and time.
The investigator preserves evidence and does not allow the alleged perpetrator or anyone involved to alter records or contact witnesses in a way that could interfere.

The investigator completes the written Investigation Report within 14 days of the initial report. The agency's Investigation Report Form is built to track 245.250(d) item by item, and the Administrator checks the form against the rule text before signing it. It states the findings and the actions taken.

If the investigation cannot be finished within 14 days because of outside actions such as a police or state investigation, the Administrator documents the reason, completes the report with what is known by day 14, and updates it when more is learned.

Within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, the Administrator sends the written report to IDPH by the method IDPH directs (IDPH Home Services Program, 217-782-7412; TTY 800-547-0466) and documents the date, time, method and confirmation of receipt.
The Administrator keeps a copy of the report and the investigation file on the premises for at least 12 months.

The Administrator decides what action to take: return to duty, retraining, discipline or termination. The decision is documented. The employee stays off direct client contact until the Administrator documents that the investigation is complete and any restriction has been lifted.
The Administrator tells the client or representative the outcome of the agency's investigation, to the extent allowed by privacy rules, and updates the service plan if needed.

The Administrator reviews each investigation at the next quality improvement meeting (GOV-04) to find ways to prevent a repeat, and checks whether the employee's conduct requires any further reporting under PER-02.

responsibilities.duty: Calls 911 or local police immediately in the situations listed and notifies the supervisor.
Removes accused employees from client contact, directs the investigation, completes the 14-day report, sends it to IDPH within 24 hours of completion and keeps copies 12 months.
Takes over the investigation when the Administrator is involved and reviews the outcome.
Protects the client, arranges replacement care and preserves records.

documentation: Record of 911 or police notification (date, time, agency, report number)
Written notice removing the employee from direct client contact
Investigation file with interview notes and records reviewed
Written Investigation Report meeting 245.250(d), completed within 14 days of the initial report
IDPH transmittal record showing the date and time sent, within 24 hours after completion
Copy of the report kept on premises for 12 months
Corrective action and outcome record

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted caregivers, supervisors and the Agency Manager of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident involving a client or worker is reported at once, documented, followed up, and reviewed for patterns. Incidents that involve suspected abuse, neglect or financial exploitation must also meet the state timelines.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires workers to observe, report and document incidents. This is a required orientation topic under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e). Every incident is reported to a supervisor immediately and documented on the Incident Report Form. Incidents include falls, injuries, property loss or damage, client elopement or wandering, worker injury, medication-reminding errors, and any other unusual event. Any incident that involves a reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation is handled under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250, SAF-01 and SAF-02. Those timelines override the routine timelines in this policy. Every incident report is reviewed in the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04). No one is disciplined or retaliated against for making a good-faith report.

definitions.definition: Any unusual or unexpected event that harms, or could have harmed, a client, worker or visitor, or that damages or removes property. Examples are a fall, injury, property loss, elopement, worker injury, a missed emergency, or a client threatening a worker.
A client who is cognitively impaired or at risk leaves the home or the care area without the knowledge or supervision needed for safety.
A belief, based on what the worker saw, heard or was told, that abuse, neglect or financial exploitation may have occurred. Proof is not required before reporting.

The agency designated by the Illinois Department on Aging, or the Area Agency on Aging, that receives reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of clients aged 60 or older and of other eligible adults under the Adult Protective Services Act (320 ILCS 20).

procedures: The worker first makes sure the client and the worker are safe. The worker gives first aid within their training and calls 911 for any emergency, then follows SVC-11.
The worker telephones the supervisor or the after-hours line [PHONE] immediately. This must be before leaving the home or within one hour of the incident, whichever is sooner.

The worker completes the Incident Report Form before the end of the shift and no later than 24 hours after the incident. The form records the date and time, the location, who was involved, what the worker saw and did, injuries or damage, who was notified, and the worker's signature.

If a worker reasonably suspects abuse, neglect or financial exploitation, the worker reports it to the supervisor or Agency Manager and also to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA, or to IDoA itself, at [ELDER ABUSE PROVIDER AGENCY PHONE]. This applies whether the client is aged 60 or older, is disabled, or is an eligible adult under 320 ILCS 20. The worker does not wait for a supervisor's approval or for the incident form to be finished. The worker reports in addition to, not instead of, the Agency Manager.
If the victim is under 18, the Agency Manager or worker calls the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-25-ABUSE (1-800-252-2873) at once.

The Agency Manager or supervisor calls 911 or local police immediately for staff-inflicted physical injury, sexual abuse by staff, a crime in the home by another person, or a death other than by disease or natural causes. The call is made before any other step.
If an employee is the alleged perpetrator, the supervisor removes that employee from direct client contact immediately and the Agency Manager starts the investigation (SAF-02).
The Agency Manager documents each abuse, neglect or exploitation report and keeps it on the agency's premises for 12 months.

The Agency Manager completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report. The report contains the elements required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250(d). It is sent to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed. A copy is kept for 12 months (SAF-02).

The supervisor reviews every other incident report within one business day. The supervisor contacts the client or the client's representative, arranges any needed medical follow-up, and notifies the emergency contact or family as the client has authorized.

For a fall or injury, the supervisor documents the client's condition, any treatment, and whether the service plan needs changing (SVC-03). The Agency Manager arranges a supervisory visit within 7 days if the client's condition or needs changed (SVC-04).

For property loss, damage or suspected theft, the supervisor takes statements from the worker and the client. The Agency Manager checks whether the loss may be financial exploitation and, if so, follows the abuse reporting steps above (CR-04).

For client elopement, the worker calls 911 immediately if the client is missing and at risk, then calls the supervisor. The supervisor notifies the emergency contact. After the client is found, the supervisor reassesses safety measures in the service plan.

For a worker injury or exposure, the worker gets medical care if needed and reports to the supervisor immediately. The supervisor completes the Incident Report Form and the workers' compensation first report of injury (GOV-09). Exposures to blood or body fluids or to a communicable illness are handled under PER-08 and SAF-04.

Where the client's payer program (IDoA Community Care Program or DHS-DRS Home Services Program) requires notice of certain incidents, the Agency Manager notifies the care coordinator or counselor within the time the program requires (SVC-13, REC-03).

The Agency Manager keeps an Incident Log and reviews it monthly for trends by client, worker, time of day and type. Each incident and the log are reviewed at the quarterly Quality Improvement meeting (GOV-04). Corrective actions are assigned, dated and tracked to completion.

The Agency Manager files the Incident Report Form in the incident file. A copy goes in the client record (REC-01), without any information about other clients. A worker's injury report is filed in the worker's confidential injury file, not the general personnel file (PER-11).
Reporting, documenting and observing incidents are taught at orientation (PER-03) and reinforced at each annual training (PER-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure safety and call 911 when needed. Report the incident to the supervisor immediately and complete the Incident Report Form within 24 hours. Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to management and to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA.
Receive reports around the clock, review each report within one business day, follow up with the client and family, and escalate to the Agency Manager.
Manage the abuse reporting and investigation timelines, notify IDPH, maintain the Incident Log, and present trends at Quality Improvement. Ensure the 12-month record retention.
Review the quarterly incident summary and require corrective action where patterns appear.

documentation: Incident Report Form (signed and dated)
Incident Log
Abuse, neglect and exploitation report records, kept on premises for 12 months
Written investigation report and the copy sent to IDPH, kept for 12 months
Supervisor follow-up notes and any service plan changes
Quality Improvement meeting minutes showing incident review
Worker injury reports and workers' compensation first report of injury

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To investigate, control and prevent infections among clients and workers in the course of non-medical in-home services.
policies.policy: This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.75, the infection control policy listed on IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item 245.75 (initial applicants only), and is submitted with the license application. [AGENCY NAME] has written policies and procedures for investigating, controlling and preventing infections, and implements them (245.75(a)). The agency follows current CDC infection-prevention guidance as it applies to in-home care, and the Agency Manager reviews 245.75(b) and the current CDC guidance at each annual policy review (GOV-03). The CDC hand-hygiene guideline handout that placement agencies must give to workers does not apply to a direct-service agency like [AGENCY NAME]. Workers are nevertheless trained in hand hygiene. Hygiene and infection control are required training topics at orientation (245.71(e)) and every year (245.71(f)). Workers use standard precautions with every client. The agency follows OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) for any worker whose job could reasonably involve contact with blood or other potentially infectious material. The influenza and pneumococcal vaccination rules for other licensed provider types do not apply to home services agencies. The agency offers workers influenza vaccination through the employee health program (PER-07, PER-08).

definitions.definition: Infection-prevention practices used with all clients regardless of known infection status: hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment when contact with body fluids is likely, safe handling of laundry and waste, cleaning of surfaces, and respiratory etiquette.
Disposable gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection used to protect the worker and the client from infection.
Contact with blood, body fluids or a communicable disease that could spread infection, such as a needlestick, splash to eyes or mouth, or close contact with a person with a reportable illness.

procedures: The Agency Manager keeps this policy and a worker infection control guide on file, and reviews both at least annually against current CDC guidance, including 245.75(b) (GOV-03).

At orientation, before first assignment, every worker is trained on hygiene and infection control. Content includes hand hygiene technique, when to wash and when to use sanitizer, glove use and removal, standard precautions, safe laundry, kitchen and bathroom cleaning, waste handling and respiratory etiquette (PER-03).

The trainer observes each worker demonstrate hand hygiene and the putting on and removal of gloves during the competency evaluation before first assignment. The result is recorded on the competency checklist (PER-04).
Every worker repeats infection control training each year as part of the 10-hour annual training (PER-05). This includes any updates from CDC or IDPH.

The agency supplies PPE (disposable gloves, masks and hand sanitizer at minimum) and a supply of disinfectant wipes. Workers receive replacement supplies from the office within one business day of a request. Workers carry supplies on every visit.

At intake, the assessor asks about any current infections, isolation instructions from a physician, or a recent hospital discharge. Findings are recorded and any precautions are written into the service plan (SVC-02, SVC-03).

Workers do not perform sterile procedures, wound care, injections, catheter care or handle sharps. If a worker finds a sharp or soiled dressing, they do not handle it with bare hands. They notify the supervisor, and the client or family arranges proper disposal.

Workers with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a rash of unknown cause, a cough with fever, or other symptoms of communicable illness do not go to a client's home. They notify the supervisor before the shift. The return-to-work rules in PER-08 apply.

A worker who has an exposure washes the area at once, reports to the supervisor immediately and completes an Incident Report Form (SAF-03). The supervisor refers the worker for medical evaluation the same day for bloodborne exposures, as required by 29 CFR 1910.1030.

Where a worker's duties could reasonably involve contact with blood or other potentially infectious material, the Agency Manager offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost after training, provides bloodborne pathogen training, and keeps the exposure records required by 29 CFR 1910.1030.

When a client has a communicable illness, the supervisor reviews the service plan with the client or representative. The supervisor adds precautions such as masks, extra cleaning or limiting visits, and informs each assigned worker before the next visit.

The Agency Manager investigates every suspected infection that may have spread between a client and a worker, or between workers. The Agency Manager records the date, persons, symptoms, contact history and actions taken in the Infection Log.

If two or more clients or workers have the same illness in a short period, the Agency Manager contacts the local health department for guidance. The Agency Manager also contacts the health department when a reportable disease is suspected and follows its direction.
Quality Improvement reviews the Infection Log at least quarterly for trends and corrective actions (GOV-04).
A worker who has a concern about a client's home hygiene reports it to the supervisor, who addresses it at the next supervisory visit (SVC-04).

responsibilities.duty: Follow standard precautions on every visit, use PPE, stay home when ill, and report exposures and symptoms immediately.
Check infection control practice at supervisory visits, supply PPE, enforce exclusion from work when symptomatic, and notify the Agency Manager of suspected infections.
Maintain this policy, review it against CDC guidance, schedule training, keep the Infection Log, and consult the local health department when needed.
Teach hygiene and infection control and verify hand-hygiene and glove skills before first assignment.

documentation: Written infection control policy and procedures (submitted with the license application)
Orientation and annual training records for hygiene and infection control
Competency checklist showing hand-hygiene and glove skills
Infection Log and exposure reports
Hepatitis B vaccine offer, acceptance or declination records, where applicable
Annual policy review record
Quality Improvement meeting minutes

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers, supervisors, and the Agency Manager of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each client has an emergency preparedness plan, that workers are trained to carry it out, and that [AGENCY NAME] can keep serving priority clients when the office closes or caregivers are unavailable.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prepares each client for emergencies and prepares the agency to keep operating. Every client has an individual emergency preparedness plan developed at intake and kept in the client record, and workers are trained on the client's plan as part of initial training (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e)). Disaster procedures are a required part of annual training (245.71(f)). Each client record holds at least one emergency contact. The agency also keeps a continuity plan covering office closure, loss of power or telephone, severe weather, public health emergencies and caregiver shortage. In any emergency, the worker calls 911 first and protects life. Workers give non-medical help only within their training.

definitions.definition: A short written plan for one client that lists emergency contacts, mobility and evacuation needs, oxygen or equipment, medication list location, utilities, pets, nearest exit, and where the client will go if the home cannot be used.
The agency's written plan for keeping essential services and communications going if the office is closed, staff are unavailable, or systems fail.
A client whose health or safety would be at serious risk if a visit were missed, such as someone who lives alone with dementia, uses oxygen, or cannot leave the home without help.

procedures: At intake, the assessor completes the Client Emergency Preparedness Plan with the client or representative. The plan records at least one emergency contact with telephone, a second contact if available, physician and pharmacy, a list of medicines and where they are kept, and known allergies (SVC-02).

The assessor records mobility, vision, hearing, cognitive and equipment needs that affect evacuation, including oxygen, wheelchair, walker and bed-bound status. The assessor also notes pets, the nearest exits, the nearest safe place in the home for severe weather, and a place to go if the client must leave.

The assessor assigns each client a priority level of high, medium or low. High means the client's safety is at serious risk if a visit is missed. The level is recorded in the record and on the schedule.
The Supervisor reviews the plan with the client at every service plan update and at every supervisory visit, and updates contacts and needs that changed (SVC-03, SVC-04).

Before first assignment, every worker is trained on the emergency procedures for the client they will serve and on how to locate the client's plan (PER-03). Training covers calling 911, first aid within the worker's training, staying with the client, and notifying the supervisor.
Every worker completes disaster procedures training each year as part of the 10-hour annual training, with first aid and emergency response refreshers (PER-05).

During a fire, severe weather, power failure, medical emergency or other event in the home, the worker calls 911 if anyone is in danger, helps the client to safety if the worker can do so without risk, stays with the client until help arrives, and then calls the supervisor. The worker completes an Incident Report Form (SAF-03).
For clients on oxygen, workers remove ignition sources, do not use open flame, and follow the plan for backup oxygen supply during a power failure (SVC-07).

The Agency Manager maintains the continuity plan, which names who will cover the office, the after-hours line and scheduling. It lists backup caregivers, and sets the order for contacting high-priority clients first when there is severe weather or an emergency (GOV-08, SVC-09).

When severe weather or a declared emergency is forecast, the Supervisor calls each high-priority client or their emergency contact before the event. The Supervisor confirms visits, arranges extra coverage, and records each contact in the client record.

If the office must close, the Agency Manager switches to the after-hours line [PHONE], contacts staff and clients by telephone or text, and keeps services going for high-priority clients. Client records and the schedule are accessible from a secure backup location (REC-02).

If a worker cannot reach a client's home because of an emergency, the worker calls the supervisor. The Supervisor tries to reach the client or emergency contact, asks for a welfare check from local police if the client is high priority and cannot be reached, and documents the attempts (SVC-09).

After any disaster or office closure, the Agency Manager holds a debrief within 14 days, updates the continuity plan and client plans as needed, and reports findings to the Quality Improvement committee (GOV-04).
The Agency Manager tests the continuity plan at least once a year through a practice call-out or tabletop exercise and records the results.

responsibilities.duty: Complete and update each client's emergency preparedness plan and priority level.
Know the client's plan, call 911 in emergencies, stay with the client, and notify the supervisor.
Maintain the continuity plan, run annual exercises, and lead the response when the office is closed.
Teach the client emergency plan at orientation and disaster procedures annually.

documentation: Client Emergency Preparedness Plan and emergency contact in each client record
Client priority level list
Orientation and annual training records for emergency and disaster procedures
Agency continuity plan and annual exercise record
Client contact log during emergencies
Post-event debrief report
Incident Report Forms

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All employees and contracted caregivers, supervisors and the Agency Manager of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To identify dangers to workers in clients' homes and in the workplace, and to protect workers from them.
policies.policy: This policy meets 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.30(c)(1)(I), the personnel policy requirement for procedures for identifying potential dangers to the health and safety of personnel providing services in the home and for protecting them from those dangers. It also meets IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, item 245.30 c) 1) I), the employee health and safety policy for initial applicants. That policy is cited with 245.30(c)(1)(H) and (I) by 245.90(a)(3)(I)(ii). Together with PER-08, which covers symptom and exposure reporting and removal from and return to client contact under 245.30(c)(1)(H), this policy satisfies that item. [AGENCY NAME] assesses each home for hazards at intake and at supervisory visits. Workers may leave any home that is unsafe and call the supervisor, and are not disciplined for doing so in good faith. Safety precautions are a required training topic under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.71(e). The agency does not tolerate violence, threats, harassment or intimidation against workers by clients, family members, visitors, co-workers or supervisors.

definitions.definition: A condition in or around a client's home that could injure a worker. Examples are aggressive pets, smoking near oxygen, firearms or other weapons, unsafe stairs or floors, pest infestations, lack of heat, a known violent person, and unsanitary conditions.
Any physical assault, threat, verbal abuse, stalking, harassment or intimidation directed at a worker while working or because of their work.
A worker's right to leave or refuse to enter a home they reasonably believe is unsafe, and to notify the supervisor.

procedures: At intake, the assessor completes the Home Safety and Worker Risk Checklist. It covers access and lighting, stairs and floors, smoking and oxygen, pets, firearms and weapons, pests, utilities, clutter, other persons in the home, history of aggression, and neighborhood or travel concerns (SVC-02).

The assessor records identified hazards and the controls agreed with the client in the service plan. Controls may include securing pets during visits, asking the client to lock up weapons, no smoking during visits, or clearing a path (SVC-03).
The Supervisor repeats the hazard check at every supervisory visit for the client and records new or changed hazards (SVC-04).
Before first assignment, the Supervisor briefs the caregiver on the client's home hazards, parking and entry, and the controls in the service plan. This is documented in the worker file.

Orientation and annual training include safety precautions, recognizing early warning signs of aggression, de-escalation, safe body mechanics and lifting limits (SVC-07), fire safety, and what to do in an unsafe situation (PER-03, PER-05).
