On receiving a report that names an employee, the Agency Manager removes the employee from direct client contact immediately, arranges coverage (SVC-09), and starts the investigation under SAF-02. The agency completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250.
The Agency Manager records each report, keeps it on the premises for 12 months, and sends the investigation report to IDPH within 24 hours of completion (SAF-02; REC-03).

The Administrator decides on discipline after the investigation. Records of the decision go in the personnel file. If the employee is cleared, the Administrator decides on return to duty and documents it.
Supervisors watch for boundary issues during supervisory visits (SVC-04, SVC-05) and in the annual evaluation (PER-12) and address them at once.
Annually, employees re-sign the conduct acknowledgment. The Agency Manager keeps the signed copies and reports any boundary violations and outcomes to the Quality Improvement Program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Follows conduct and boundary rules, declines gifts and financial dealings, and reports suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately.
Monitors conduct, documents and addresses boundary issues, and receives and escalates reports.
Trains staff, removes alleged perpetrators from client contact, ensures investigations and required reports are completed, and keeps records.
Decides discipline and ensures no retaliation.

documentation: Signed conduct and mandated-reporter acknowledgments (initial and annual)
Gift or boundary event notes (CR-04)
Abuse, neglect and exploitation reports and written investigation reports, kept on premises for 12 months
Records of removal from client contact and return to duty
Disciplinary records in the personnel file

policies.title: Contracted Staff and Third-Party Providers
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Agency Manager, supervisors, human resources and scheduling staff, and every contracted worker or third-party provider who delivers services for [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that any worker or provider [AGENCY NAME] uses by contract is properly credentialed, screened, trained, supervised and covered by a written contract, so that clients receive the same safe, compliant service as they would from an agency employee.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may deliver services directly or through written contracts with third-party providers, as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(a)-(b) permits. The agency stays responsible for the quality and safety of every contracted service. A contracted worker must hold any license, registration or certification the work requires, and the agency supervises that worker (245.30(c)(5)). Contracted workers meet the same health care worker background check, registry, training, competency and employee health standards as agency employees. No contracted worker may begin a client assignment until the agency has verified these items. Every third-party contract must be in writing and contain the nine required elements: (1) services to be provided; (2) adherence to agency policies and personnel requirements; (3) agency control over the services; (4) service notes; (5) charges; (6) liability and insurance; (7) term; (8) signatures; and (9) termination (245.210(b)). The agency does not use a contracted worker for any task outside the scope of work in SVC-01.

definitions.definition: An individual or business, not on the agency's payroll as an employee, that provides home services to agency clients under a written contract with [AGENCY NAME].
The agency's authority to assign, direct, supervise, evaluate and end the contracted worker's services to its clients.
Any State professional license, registry listing or certification a particular task or role requires by law.

procedures: Before engaging any contractor, the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] decides which services will be contracted and confirms they are on the agency's written list of services and scope of work (SVC-01).
Human resources collects the contractor's identifying information, evidence of qualifications and any license, registration or certification the role requires.

For any role that requires a State professional license, human resources verifies with IDFPR that the license is active, prints the verification and files it in the contractor's personnel file before the first assignment (245.30(c)).

Human resources runs the fingerprint-based background check and Health Care Worker Registry check for each individual contracted worker and does not schedule the worker until results are cleared (PER-02).

If the contractor is a business with its own workers, the contract requires the business to run the same checks. The agency obtains and keeps written proof for each worker who will enter a client's home.

The Administrator confirms each contracted worker has completed the same orientation, initial training, dementia training where applicable, and competency evaluation required of agency employees, or completes that training through the agency before first assignment (PER-03, PER-04, SVC-08).
Each contracted worker completes the initial health evaluation and TB screening required for employees and follows the illness and exposure reporting rules (PER-07, PER-08).

The Administrator and the contractor sign a written contract that includes all nine required elements: services, adherence to agency policies and personnel requirements, agency control, notes, charges, liability and insurance, term, signatures and termination.

The contract requires the contractor to follow this Policy and Procedure Manual, to use agency visit documentation forms or the EVV system, and to submit service notes on the agency's schedule (REC-04, SVC-10).
The contract states the contractor's insurance and liability coverage. Human resources obtains a certificate of insurance and calendars its expiration date (GOV-09).
The contract states that the agency may remove a contracted worker from any client assignment at any time and sets out termination conditions for both parties.
A supervisor assigns each contracted worker to the same supervisory visit and annual observation schedule as employees (SVC-04, SVC-05).

The contracted worker follows the agency's reporting rules for abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents and changes in client condition. The contract requires immediate reporting to the supervisor (SAF-01, SAF-03, SVC-11).
Human resources repeats the registry verification annually and re-checks any required license or certification at each renewal date for the duration of the contract (PER-05).
The Administrator reviews each contract at least annually and at renewal, and reviews contractor performance as part of quality improvement (GOV-04, PER-12).

Human resources keeps the signed contract, license verification, background and registry results, training and competency records, and insurance certificate in a contractor file, kept as personnel records (PER-11).

responsibilities.duty: Approves all contracts, signs for the agency, and ensures contracted workers are supervised and meet every personnel requirement before first assignment.
Verifies licenses and registry status, runs background checks, gathers insurance proof, and maintains contractor files.
Supervise and observe contracted workers, review their notes, and report concerns to the Administrator.
Meets all qualifications, follows agency policies, documents each visit, and reports incidents and suspected abuse immediately.

documentation: Signed written contract with all nine required elements
IDFPR license verification (where a license is required) and copy of license, registration or certification
Background check and Health Care Worker Registry results, with annual registry verification
Training, competency evaluation and employee health records
Certificate of insurance
Supervisory visit and annual observation records
Contractor performance review notes

policies.title: Wage, Hour and Overtime Compliance
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Agency Manager, payroll and scheduling staff, supervisors, and all caregivers and other hourly employees
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] pays every employee lawfully for all hours worked, including travel between clients and required training, and clearly tells clients who the employer is and who pays employment taxes and workers' compensation.
policies.policy: Home care workers employed by [AGENCY NAME] are covered by the federal Fair Labor Standards Act minimum wage and overtime rules (29 CFR 552) and by Illinois wage laws. The agency pays at least the highest applicable minimum wage (federal, State, county or municipal) for every hour worked, and pays overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Time spent traveling between clients during the workday, and time spent in required orientation and training, is paid working time. Minimum wage rates for the State, Cook County and the City of Chicago change, and the figures available when this manual was written came from secondary sources that conflict for Chicago. The Administrator therefore confirms current rates with the Illinois Department of Labor (IDOL) and the City of Chicago, and re-checks them every July 1 and January 1. The client agreement states who is the employer, who pays employment taxes and Social Security taxes, and who provides workers' compensation (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(c)). Caregivers working for the agency are employees, and the agency does not treat them as independent contractors.

definitions.definition: All time an employee is required or permitted to work, including client visits, paid travel between clients, required training, orientation, and required meetings.
A fixed, recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods), set by the agency at [WORKWEEK START DAY AND TIME], used to measure overtime.
The hourly rate of pay, plus certain other payments, used to calculate the overtime premium.
The highest of the federal, Illinois, county and municipal minimum wage rates that applies to the work location.

procedures: The Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates a payroll lead and keeps a written wage scale that sets each position's pay at or above the applicable minimum wage (PER-09).

Each January and July, before the 1st, the payroll lead confirms current minimum wage rates with IDOL and the City of Chicago, and with Cook County where it applies, and records the date checked and the sources. The agency raises any pay rate that falls below the new minimum by its effective date.
The agency sets and records the workweek in writing and applies it consistently to all employees.
Caregivers record actual start and end times for every visit, using the EVV system where required, or the agency timesheet (SVC-10, REC-04).

Payroll counts travel time between one client's home and the next during a workday as paid time. Payroll pays the same hourly rate or a lawfully calculated blended rate, and records the travel time separately from visit time.
Scheduling staff build schedules that account for travel time and tell caregivers how to record it.

Payroll pays for all orientation, initial training, annual training, competency evaluations and required meetings at the employee's regular rate. Human resources records the hours in the training record (PER-03, PER-05, PER-06).
Payroll reviews each week's hours before payroll closes. It flags any employee approaching 40 hours and tells the supervisor and scheduling.

Payroll pays overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in the workweek. Supervisors may not tell employees to work off the clock, edit time to avoid overtime, or delay recording time.

Scheduling staff and supervisors obtain approval from the Administrator before scheduling planned overtime, except where needed to protect a client's safety. Overtime that is worked is always paid, whether or not it was approved.
Employees must report any pay error to payroll immediately. Payroll investigates within [NUMBER] business days and corrects underpayments on the next pay date or sooner.
Payroll pays employees on a regular pay schedule set in the personnel policies, and gives each employee a written pay statement showing hours, rate and deductions (PER-09).

Before service starts, the client agreement tells the client who the employer is, who pays employment taxes and Social Security taxes, who provides workers' compensation, and who supervises, hires, fires and disciplines workers (CR-06, GOV-09).

The Administrator reviews payroll practices at least annually, and again after any change in law or any wage complaint. The Administrator may consult employment counsel and corrects any problems found.
Payroll keeps time and payroll records for the period required by federal and State law and stores them as personnel records (PER-11).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures lawful pay practices, approves wage scales, and confirms minimum wage rates each January and July.
Calculates pay, travel time, training time and overtime; corrects errors; keeps payroll records.
Schedule within overtime limits, account for travel time, and never allow off-the-clock work.
Record all time accurately and report pay errors right away.

documentation: Written wage scale and minimum wage verification log (date, source, rates) updated each January and July
Timesheets and EVV time records
Payroll registers and pay statements
Training and orientation hour records
Overtime approvals
Pay error reports and corrections
Client agreement language on employer, taxes and workers' compensation

policies.title: Client Records Content and Retention
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Agency Manager, office and records staff, supervisors and caregivers who create or handle client records
policies.purpose: To define what [AGENCY NAME] keeps in each client record, how long records are retained, and in what form, so that records are complete, available to the agency and to IDPH surveyors, and kept for the required period.
policies.policy: This policy meets 245.210 h) (IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, applicable to initial applicants only: client records management and release requirements). It is the agency's written records policy, and REC-02 completes it with the use, removal and release rules. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every client. Each record holds: (1) identifying information; (2) contact information for the client's representative, if any; (3) an emergency contact; (4) the agreed service plan; (5) the signed home care services agreement; and (6) worker documentation of each service at each visit (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(h)). This content matches the definition of client record in 245.20, which covers personal information, emergency notification information, agreed service plans, the home services contract, and documentation of services at each visit. Records are kept at least 2 years after the last date of service, in hard copy or electronic form. If a payer contract or other law requires a longer period, the longer period applies. Any faxed record is received or kept on non-thermal paper.

definitions.definition: The agency's file for a client holding personal information, emergency notification information, agreed service plans, the home services contract, and documentation of services at each visit.
The date of the final visit or service delivered to a client; the retention period runs from this date.
Plain paper that does not fade over time, as opposed to thermal fax paper, which fades.
A person the client has named, or who is legally authorized, to act for the client.

procedures: At intake, the intake coordinator opens a client record in hard copy, electronic form or both, and assigns it a unique client identifier (SVC-02).
The intake coordinator records the client's identifying information: full name, address, telephone number, date of birth and payer source.
The intake coordinator records the representative's name and contact information, with the document showing the person's authority if one exists, or notes that there is no representative.
The intake coordinator records at least one emergency contact with telephone number and relationship, and confirms it with the client (SAF-05).
The supervisor places the agreed service plan in the record before services begin and each time it is updated, with dates and signatures (SVC-03).
Before services begin, the Administrator or designee ensures the signed home care services agreement, with the list of services and scope of work, is filed in the record (CR-06).
The supervisor adds the assessment, authorizations or referral from CCP or HSP where applicable, and consent and authorization forms (SVC-02, SVC-13).
Caregivers document each service at each visit, and the office files the visit documentation in the record, either as paper notes or in the electronic system, on the schedule in REC-04.
Supervisors file supervisory visit notes, change-in-condition reports, incident reports and notices of discharge or transfer in the record (SVC-04, SVC-11, SAF-03, SVC-12).
Records staff checks each new record within [NUMBER] business days of start of care against a content checklist for all six required items, and notes gaps for the supervisor to correct.
The Administrator audits a sample of records each quarter for completeness and timely visit documentation as part of the quality improvement program (GOV-04).

Staff keep personnel information, such as caregiver background check results, out of the client record unless it is part of the service plan. Records on abuse or neglect investigations are kept as separate files under SAF-02, retained at least 12 months.

When a client is discharged, the supervisor records the last date of service and the records staff marks the file closed and writes the earliest destruction date, which is 2 years after that date, or later where a payer contract or other law requires it (SVC-12).
Records staff keeps closed records in secure storage, retrievable for the IDPH surveyor or payer on request, until the destruction date.

After the retention period ends, and after the Administrator confirms there is no open complaint, investigation, audit or legal hold, records staff destroys the record by shredding paper or permanently deleting electronic files, and logs the destruction.
The agency accepts faxed records only on non-thermal paper. If a document arrives on thermal paper, records staff photocopies it onto plain paper and files the copy.
Electronic records are backed up regularly, and the agency can print or show a readable copy of any record promptly on request (REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Owns the records policy, audits record completeness, and authorizes record destruction.
Opens the record and enters identifying, representative and emergency contact information.
File service plans, supervisory notes and change-in-condition documents, and correct gaps.
Maintains files, checks completeness, handles retention, storage, and destruction.
Document each service at each visit completely and accurately.

documentation: Client record with all six required content items
Record completeness checklist and audit results
Closed-record log with last date of service and earliest destruction date
Destruction log
Backup records for electronic files

policies.title: Client Records Management, Use and Release
policies.applies_to: All employees, contracted workers, volunteers and any person with access to client records at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of client records and to set the rules for how records are used, removed from the office and released to others.
policies.policy: This policy meets 245.210 h) (IDPH Form 445104, p. 8, applicable to initial applicants only: client records management and release requirements). It is the agency's written confidentiality policy required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.210(j), covering the use, removal and release of client records. Client records are used only by people who need them to deliver, supervise, bill for or oversee services. The agency stores records so that their confidentiality is protected, in locked cabinets and in password-protected systems. Records may not be removed from the office, except as this policy allows. The agency releases records only with a written authorization signed by the client or the client's representative, unless the law requires or permits release without it. The agency follows the HIPAA minimum necessary standard and the general disclosure rule in 45 CFR 164.502 to the extent they apply (see CR-03 for the full privacy policy). Anyone who violates this policy is subject to discipline, up to and including termination.

definitions.definition: A signed, dated written permission from the client or representative that names what may be released, to whom, and for what purpose, and states how and when it expires or may be revoked.
Sharing, reviewing or applying client information within the agency for service, supervision, billing or quality purposes.
Giving client information to a person or organization outside the agency.
Taking a client record or part of it out of the agency office, in paper or electronic form.

procedures: The Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] assigns each staff role a level of record access (for example, caregivers see the service plan and visit notes of assigned clients only) and keeps this list in writing.
Every employee, contractor and volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement at hire, before any access to client information, and again at each annual evaluation (PER-11, PER-12).

Records staff stores paper records in locked cabinets in a locked or access-controlled area. Electronic records require individual user names, passwords and automatic log-off. Records staff disables access the same day a person leaves the agency or changes roles.
Staff do not discuss clients in public areas and do not leave records unattended on desks, in vehicles or in the client's home.

Staff may not remove records from the office, except: (a) the service plan and visit documentation forms a caregiver needs at the client's home; (b) records needed for a supervisory visit; and (c) records an authorized person takes under the Administrator's written approval. Staff log each removal and return.
Records that leave the office stay in the staff member's control, are not left in a vehicle or shared space, and are returned to the office as soon as the need ends.

For a request from the client or representative to see or copy the record, records staff verifies identity and authority, then provides access or copies within the time required by law and [AGENCY NAME]'s procedures. Records staff logs the request and what was provided.

For release to any other person or organization, records staff first obtains a written authorization signed by the client or representative, checks that it is valid, and releases only the information it names.

Without authorization, records staff may release records only where the law requires or permits: to IDPH during a survey or complaint investigation, to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA or law enforcement in connection with abuse reports, to the CCP or HSP payer for authorization, billing and audit under the payer's contract, and to emergency responders when needed to protect the client's health or safety. The Administrator approves each such release, or the supervisor does in an emergency.
Records staff releases only the minimum necessary information, labels the release with the recipient and the date, and records every release in a disclosure log in the client record.

Records staff sends records by fax only after confirming the recipient's number and that the recipient is ready to receive. Faxed copies are on non-thermal paper. Email or electronic transfer is used only with encryption or another secure method.

Staff who suspect that a record was lost, stolen or released improperly report it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates, takes corrective action, and gives any notice required under HIPAA or other law (CR-03, SAF-03).
The Administrator reviews the access list and the removal and disclosure logs at least once each quarter and corrects problems.
Records staff retains and destroys records according to REC-01, and uses shredding or secure deletion so the information cannot be read or recovered.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, approves access levels and non-routine releases, investigates breaches.
Verifies authorizations, releases records, keeps removal and disclosure logs, and secures storage.
Make sure that staff they supervise follow these rules, and report violations.
Use records only as needed for their jobs, sign the confidentiality agreement, and report any loss or improper disclosure.

documentation: Signed confidentiality agreements
Role-based access list
Signed client or representative authorizations
Record removal and return log
Disclosure log in each client record
Breach investigation reports and corrective actions
Quarterly access review notes

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Agency Manager, supervisors, records staff, and any employee who learns of a reportable event or a change affecting the license
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] sends every report and notice the State requires to IDPH and other designated agencies, on time, and keeps proof that it did.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] meets the following State reporting requirements. (1) Abuse, neglect and financial exploitation: staff report a reasonable suspicion to the elder abuse provider agency designated by IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging (for victims aged 60 or older, disabled clients and eligible adults) or to the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline (for a victim under 18). The agency completes a written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report, sends it to IDPH within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, and keeps a copy for 12 months (77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.250). (2) Changes: the agency notifies IDPH within 10 days of any change, using the Facility Information Change Form. (3) New counties: the agency obtains IDPH approval before it serves clients in a new county. (4) Licensing: the agency tracks its provisional license (valid 240 days, extendable 120 days where it shows substantial progress, 245.100) and the compliance survey that takes place within 30 days of the provisional license expiration, and it submits its renewal application before the full license expires. IDPH Form 445104 instructs renewal applicants to apply 60 days before expiration, and the agency follows that timeline. The agency also complies with all payer reporting requirements in its CCP and HSP contracts.

definitions.definition: A reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect or financial exploitation of a client, as defined in SAF-01.
The IDPH form the agency uses to notify IDPH of a change in its licensing information.
The initial license, valid for 240 days and extendable by 120 days, that precedes the full license.
The first report of a suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to management or to the elder abuse provider agency or IDoA; the 14-day investigation clock starts here.

procedures: The Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] keeps a regulatory calendar listing every deadline: the provisional license expiration date, the survey window, the full license expiration date and the renewal submission date, which is 60 days before expiration, plus certificate and contract renewals.

Any employee or volunteer who suspects abuse, neglect or financial exploitation reports it to the supervisor or Administrator immediately and also to the elder abuse provider agency, IDoA or the Area Agency on Aging. For a victim under 18, staff call the DCFS Child Abuse Hotline. Staff call 911 or local police immediately where the law requires it (SAF-01, SAF-02).
The Administrator or designee records each report on the abuse report log: date, time, who reported, who received the report, and the agency's follow-up. Reports are kept on premises for 12 months.
If an employee is the alleged perpetrator, the Administrator removes that employee from direct client contact immediately and starts the investigation (SAF-02).

The investigator completes the written investigation report within 14 days of the initial report. The report includes all six elements required by 245.250(d), and the Administrator reviews and signs it.

Within 24 hours after the investigation is completed, the Administrator sends the investigation report to IDPH, using the IDPH Home Services Program contact in the licensing file (phone 217-782-7412, email DPH.COOS@illinois.gov), and keeps proof of transmission. The agency keeps a copy of the report for 12 months.
The Administrator continues to meet mandated-reporter duties under the Adult Protective Services Act, which apply in addition to the reports above.

For any change affecting the license information on file with IDPH, such as a change of address, telephone, administrator, ownership or services, the employee who learns of it informs the Administrator right away. The Administrator completes the Facility Information Change Form and submits it to IDPH no later than 10 days after the change, and keeps the confirmation (GOV-07).

Before accepting a client in a county not already approved, the Administrator submits the request to IDPH and gets IDPH's written approval. Intake does not accept clients in the new county until approval is on file (GOV-02, GOV-07).

The Administrator checks the calendar monthly. Beginning 120 days before the full license expiration, the Administrator gathers the renewal materials, including the application and the $1,500 fee by check or money order (electronic payment is not accepted, and the fee is non-refundable).
The Administrator submits the renewal application 60 days before the full license expires, as Form 445104 instructs, and keeps proof of the submission date.

During the provisional license period, the Administrator tracks the 240-day term. If the agency has made substantial progress but cannot finish, the Administrator applies for the 120-day extension in time. The agency prepares for the compliance survey that takes place within 30 days of provisional expiration (GOV-06).
The Administrator follows reporting requirements in the agency's CCP and HSP contracts, and applicable payer rules for incidents and EVV compliance (SVC-13, SVC-10, SAF-03).

Each quarter, the Administrator reviews the regulatory calendar, abuse report log and change log against what was filed, and corrects any missed or late report immediately and records the reason (GOV-04).

The Administrator keeps copies of all reports, notices, transmission proofs and IDPH responses in a regulatory file, retained at least as long as the retention period for each item, and no less than 12 months for abuse reports and investigation reports.

responsibilities.duty: Submits all reports and notices to IDPH, maintains the regulatory calendar, and signs investigation reports.
Receive reports from caregivers, begin the log entry, and alert the Administrator immediately.
Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, and tell the Administrator of any change affecting the license.
Maintains the abuse report log, change log and the regulatory file.

documentation: Regulatory calendar (license, survey and renewal dates)
Abuse report log and written investigation reports with IDPH transmission proof
Facility Information Change Forms with confirmations
IDPH approval for each new county
Renewal application, fee payment record and proof of submission
Quarterly regulatory review notes

policies.title: Caregiver Visit Documentation
policies.applies_to: All caregivers (home services workers), contracted workers, supervisors, and office staff who review visit notes and bill for services
policies.purpose: To ensure caregivers document the services they provide at each visit completely, accurately and on time, so the client record is complete, supervisors can review care, and billing is supported.
policies.policy: Home services workers document the services they provide, as 77 Ill. Adm. Code 245.40(c) provides. The client record must contain worker documentation of each service at each visit (245.210(h); client record definition in 245.20). Every visit is documented. Visit notes become part of the client record and support billing: the agency bills only for visits that are documented and, where required, verified by EVV. Supervisors review visit notes at supervisory visits. Notes describe what the caregiver actually did and observed, in factual language, within the tasks on the client's service plan. Caregivers also observe and report changes in client functioning, and they never record or perform tasks outside the scope in SVC-01.

definitions.definition: The caregiver's record of one visit: date, times, tasks performed, and observations, signed by the caregiver.
A factual description of what the caregiver saw, heard or was told about the client's condition or functioning, without diagnosing.
A note written after the visit ended, clearly marked as late with the actual date and time it was written.
The list of tasks agreed to in the client's service plan, which the visit note is matched against.

procedures: Before the first visit, the supervisor gives each caregiver the client's service plan task list and the agency's visit note form or electronic visit documentation tool, and shows the caregiver how to use it (SVC-03).
At the start of each visit, the caregiver clocks in using EVV where required or records the actual start time on the visit note (SVC-10).

During the visit, the caregiver provides only the services on the service plan and records each task done, such as assistance with ADLs and personal care, meal preparation, housekeeping, laundry, shopping, escort to appointments and companionship.

The caregiver notes any task on the plan that was not done or was refused by the client, with the reason, and any extra help the client requested that is outside the plan, so the supervisor can follow up.
The caregiver records observations of changes in client functioning, appetite, mood, mobility, skin, or the home environment, in factual terms, and does not diagnose or interpret.

The caregiver reports a significant change in condition, an injury, a fall, or any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the supervisor immediately by phone, and does not rely on the visit note alone (SVC-11, SAF-01, SAF-03).
If the caregiver gave medication reminders, the note records the reminder given and the client's response only, and not any administration (SVC-06).

At the end of each visit, before leaving the home, the caregiver records the actual end time, signs and dates the note, and clocks out using EVV where required. The caregiver does not complete or sign notes before the visit is done, and does not copy notes from previous visits.
Where the agency requires client or representative acknowledgment, the caregiver asks for the signature or electronic confirmation and records if the client is unable or declines.
The caregiver turns in or uploads visit notes to the office by [DAY AND TIME DEADLINE], no later than [NUMBER] days after the visit.

If a caregiver needs to correct a note, the caregiver draws a single line through the error, writes the correction, and initials and dates it. In an electronic system, the caregiver adds a dated correction and does not delete the original. Staff never alter or backdate another person's note.
If the caregiver forgot to document something, the caregiver writes a late entry marked with the actual date and time of writing and gives the reason.

Records staff reviews notes when received for completeness: date, times, tasks, observations and signatures. It matches them with the schedule and EVV data, and returns incomplete notes to the caregiver for correction within [NUMBER] business day(s).

Records staff files the notes in the client record (REC-01). Billing staff bills only for visits with complete, matching documentation, and holds any visit with missing or inconsistent notes until it is resolved (GOV-05).

At each supervisory visit, the supervisor reviews recent visit notes with the service plan, looks for missing tasks, repeated refusals or reported changes, and follows up with the caregiver and client. The supervisor records the review in the supervisory visit note (SVC-04, SVC-05).

The Administrator audits a sample of visit notes against EVV data and billing each quarter as part of quality improvement, and retrains caregivers or takes corrective action where documentation is deficient (GOV-04, PER-12).

responsibilities.duty: Document each visit accurately and on time, report changes and concerns immediately, and never falsify or pre-fill notes.
Teach documentation standards, review notes at supervisory visits, and follow up on problems.
Check notes for completeness, file them in the client record, and return incomplete notes for correction.
Bill only documented visits, and audit notes against EVV and billing quarterly.

documentation: Signed visit notes for every visit (paper or electronic)
EVV records matched to notes
Late entry and correction records
Supervisory visit notes showing visit note review
Quarterly documentation and billing audit results

official.notes: The application has no numbered items. It uses a bulleted checklist, and each line carries a regulatory cite in parentheses, which I used as the item ID. The policies are due with an initial application, mailed to IDPH with the $1,500 fee (the form says electronic submission is not accepted). The checklist does not require the manual to follow any set order or category scheme, so mirroring the checklist order is a sensible way to organize it. IDPH surveyors later ask to see the 'Policy and Procedure Manuals' (surveillance checklist). I left out these checklist lines as non-policy paperwork: proof of general liability coverage ($1M per occurrence / $3M aggregate, 245.90(a)(2)), proof of Health Care Worker Registry access (955.115), and the Attachment E manager qualification form. The fee schedule is also not listed as a policy item. Gaps: (1) The full text of 245.30(c)(1)(E)-(G), 245.40(c) and 245.210(e)-(h) was not retrievable in full, so I did not list items I could not confirm. Check the full Part 245 text on the JCAR site for those. (2) The application's checklist cites only 245.30(c)(1)(I) for employee health and safety, while 245.90(a)(3)(I)(ii) cites both (H) and (I), so cover both. (3) For Alzheimer's/dementia training, see 245.211 and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 973, which the surveillance checklist asks for. This is a training curriculum, not a policy checklist item. (4) Agencies serving only CCP, DHS-DRS or VA clients may be excluded from IDPH licensure (245.20), and the application's client counts exclude those clients.
